about: Neuroscience and Behaviour is a shared UK-wide revision pack, not one university's syllabus. It supports preclinical neuroscience courses (for example second-year neurobiology and human behaviour, systems and cellular neuroscience) and clinical neuroscience placements in later years. It runs from neurons and synapses through neuroanatomy, sensory, motor and autonomic systems and higher cortical function to neuropharmacology and the common neurological disorders listed in the GMC's MLA content map. Clinical guidance points are checked against current UK sources (NICE, MHRA, RCP, Resuscitation Council UK). This pack is educational revision material, not clinical advice, and gives no drug doses.

notes.h: Neurons, membrane potentials and synaptic transmission
notes.overview: Neurons signal electrically along their membranes and chemically across synapses. This topic explains why the resting membrane sits near the potassium equilibrium potential, how voltage-gated channels generate and propagate the action potential, how transmitter release and receptor type set the speed and sign of a synapse, and how these mechanisms explain common clinical problems.
objectives: Explain why the resting membrane potential lies close to E_K, using the Nernst equation.
Describe the ionic basis of the action potential and of the absolute and relative refractory periods.
Explain how myelin and axon diameter increase conduction velocity.
Distinguish ionotropic from metabotropic receptors and EPSPs from IPSPs.
Apply membrane physiology to hyperkalaemia, demyelination and botulinum toxin.

sections.h: Neurons, glia and the resting potential
sections.body:
A neuron receives input on its dendrites and cell body (soma). Its axon begins at the axon hillock and initial segment, where inputs are summed and action potentials usually start, and ends in presynaptic terminals. Glia support neurons:
- Astrocytes help form the blood–brain barrier, buffer extracellular K⁺ and take up glutamate.
- Oligodendrocytes myelinate segments of several CNS axons; each Schwann cell myelinates one segment of a single peripheral axon.
- Microglia are the resident immune cells; ependymal cells line the ventricles.
The resting membrane potential is typically about −70 mV (it varies between cells). At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, so the potential sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential. The Nernst equation gives each ion's equilibrium potential: at 37 °C, for a monovalent cation, E ≈ 61.5 log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV. With K⁺ 5 mM outside and 140 mM inside, E_K ≈ 61.5 × log₁₀(0.036) ≈ −89 mV. A small Na⁺ leak pulls the resting potential slightly less negative than E_K; the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation weights each ion by its permeability. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) maintains the gradients but contributes only a few millivolts directly.

- Depolarisation to threshold (about −55 mV) opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. Na⁺ enters, driving the membrane towards E_Na (about +60 mV). This is positive feedback, so the spike is all-or-none.
- Within about a millisecond the Na⁺ channels' inactivation gates close, and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ leaves and the membrane repolarises. Because the K⁺ channels close late, there is a brief afterhyperpolarisation.
- Absolute refractory period: inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen, so no second spike is possible. Relative refractory period: a stronger stimulus is needed. Refractoriness makes propagation one-way and limits firing frequency.
- Conduction velocity rises with axon diameter (lower internal resistance) and with myelin. Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so local current spreads further; the action potential is regenerated only at nodes of Ranvier, where Na⁺ channels cluster (saltatory conduction).

At a chemical synapse the arriving action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle fusion (Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin; SNARE proteins such as synaptobrevin, syntaxin and SNAP-25 drive fusion) and transmitter is released by exocytosis.
- Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels giving fast responses (nicotinic ACh, AMPA, GABA-A). Metabotropic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers and give slower, longer-lasting effects (muscarinic, GABA-B, most monoamine receptors).
- An EPSP moves the membrane towards threshold; an IPSP moves it away (or clamps it near rest, e.g. Cl⁻ entry through GABA-A channels).
- EPSPs and IPSPs sum spatially (different synapses) and temporally (repeated input) at the initial segment.
- Transmitter action ends by reuptake (glutamate, GABA, monoamines), enzymatic breakdown (acetylcholinesterase) or diffusion.
NMDA glutamate receptors conduct only when glutamate and the co-agonist glycine are bound and the membrane is depolarised enough to expel Mg²⁺ from the pore. They admit Ca²⁺, which triggers long-term potentiation (first described by Bliss and Lømo in 1973). LTP is a leading candidate mechanism for learning, but direct proof that it underlies memory is still debated.

- Hyperkalaemia raises extracellular K⁺, so E_K and the resting potential become less negative. A modest rise makes cells more excitable, but sustained depolarisation leaves many Na⁺ channels inactivated, so excitability and conduction fall. In the heart this shows as peaked T waves and, later, broad QRS complexes and dangerous arrhythmias.
- Demyelination slows or blocks conduction: in the CNS in multiple sclerosis, in peripheral nerves in Guillain–Barré syndrome. Warmth can worsen conduction in demyelinated axons (Uhthoff's phenomenon).
- Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins in cholinergic terminals, preventing acetylcholine release and causing descending flaccid paralysis.
- Myasthenia gravis is the postsynaptic counterpart: antibodies reduce functional acetylcholine receptors, so transmission fails with repeated use (fatigable weakness).
- Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; small-diameter fibres (pain, temperature, autonomic) tend to be blocked earlier than large motor fibres.

- Students often think the Na⁺/K⁺ pump "generates" the resting potential. In fact the potential arises mainly from K⁺ diffusing out through leak channels down the gradient the pump maintains; the pump's direct electrogenic share is only a few millivolts.
- Students often think a bigger stimulus gives a bigger action potential. Above threshold the spike is all-or-none; intensity is coded by firing frequency and by how many neurons are recruited.
- Students often think hyperpolarisation causes the absolute refractory period. It is Na⁺ channel inactivation that does this.
- Students often think an IPSP must hyperpolarise. Shunting inhibition through Cl⁻ channels can hold the membrane near rest without much change in voltage, yet still cancel EPSPs.
- Students often think NMDA receptors respond to glutamate alone. They also need glycine (or D-serine) and depolarisation to relieve the Mg²⁺ block, which is why they act as coincidence detectors.

notes.h: Neuroanatomy overview: organisation, blood supply and CSF
notes.overview: Clinical neurology is largely localisation: working out where a lesion is from what it does. This topic gives the map: the parts of the brain and spinal cord, the arterial territories that explain stroke patterns, and the CSF pathway that explains hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure.
objectives: Describe the main divisions of the CNS and the functions of each lobe.
Explain the territories of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries and predict the deficit from each.
Trace CSF from production to absorption and distinguish communicating from non-communicating hydrocephalus.
Explain why a small internal capsule lesion can cause a dense hemiparesis.
Apply the Oxford (Bamford) classification to a stroke presentation.

sections.body:
The CNS comprises the cerebral hemispheres, diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus), brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), cerebellum and spinal cord.
- Each hemisphere has frontal (motor, executive), parietal (somatosensory, spatial), temporal (auditory, memory) and occipital (visual) lobes; the insula lies deep in the lateral sulcus.
- The central sulcus separates the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) from the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex). The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
- White matter: association fibres (within a hemisphere, e.g. arcuate fasciculus), commissural fibres (between hemispheres, e.g. corpus callosum) and projection fibres (to and from lower centres, e.g. internal capsule).
- Basal ganglia: caudate and putamen (striatum), globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra.
- Thalamus relays most sensory input to the cortex; hypothalamus directs autonomic and endocrine control.
- Cranial nerve nuclei: III and IV in the midbrain; V (main sensory and motor), VI, VII and VIII in the pons; IX, X and XII in the medulla.
- Spinal cord: dorsal horn sensory, ventral horn motor, lateral horn autonomic (thoracic, upper lumbar and sacral levels). In adults the cord usually ends around L1–L2 (conus medullaris), with the cauda equina below.

The internal carotid arteries give the anterior (ACA) and middle (MCA) cerebral arteries. The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which supplies the brainstem and cerebellum and ends as the two posterior cerebral arteries (PCA). Anterior and posterior communicating arteries complete the circle of Willis, which can partly compensate when one inflow is blocked; its anatomy varies between people.
- ACA: medial surface of the hemisphere, including the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex. Occlusion causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss affecting the leg more than face and arm.
- MCA: most of the lateral surface, including face and arm areas and, in the dominant hemisphere, language areas. Its deep lenticulostriate branches supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness more than leg, sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, and aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant).
- PCA: occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal lobe. Occlusion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
- The posterior limb of the internal capsule packs corticospinal fibres for face, arm and leg into a small area, so a small lacunar infarct there can cause a dense pure motor hemiparesis.

CSF is produced mainly by the choroid plexus in the ventricles (roughly 500 mL a day, with about 150 mL present at any time; approximate). It flows:
- lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina (of Monro) → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinuses.
The meninges are dura, arachnoid and pia. Blood can collect in different compartments: extradural (usually arterial, classically middle meningeal artery after a temporal fracture), subdural (bridging veins, often older people or after minor trauma) and subarachnoid (usually a ruptured berry aneurysm near the circle of Willis).
Obstruction within the ventricular system (e.g. aqueduct stenosis, a posterior fossa mass) causes non-communicating hydrocephalus; impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations (e.g. after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis) causes communicating hydrocephalus. Because the skull is rigid, a rising volume of blood, brain or CSF eventually raises intracranial pressure; late signs include falling consciousness and the Cushing response (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing).

A 74-year-old has sudden right arm and face weakness, a right homonymous hemianopia and difficulty finding words. Face and arm affected more than the leg, plus language disturbance, points to the left MCA territory. Using the Oxford (Bamford) classification, a total anterior circulation syndrome needs all three of: unilateral weakness or sensory loss of at least two of face, arm and leg; homonymous hemianopia; and higher cortical dysfunction (such as dysphasia or visuospatial disorder). Any two of these (or higher cortical dysfunction alone) is a partial anterior circulation syndrome. Lacunar syndromes (pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor or ataxic hemiparesis) have no cortical signs. Posterior circulation syndromes include cranial nerve palsy with contralateral motor or sensory deficit, bilateral deficits, conjugate gaze disorders, cerebellar signs or isolated homonymous hemianopia.
By contrast, weakness mainly of one leg with little arm involvement suggests the contralateral ACA, and a hemianopia without weakness suggests the PCA.

- Students often think an MCA stroke typically causes leg-predominant weakness. The leg area sits on the medial surface (ACA territory), so MCA strokes affect the face and arm more than the leg.
- Students often think a small stroke can only cause a small deficit. A small lacune in the internal capsule or pons can cause a dense hemiparesis because so many fibres are packed together.

notes.body:
Organisation of the CNS
The CNS comprises the cerebral hemispheres, diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus), brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), cerebellum and spinal cord.
- Each hemisphere has frontal (motor, executive), parietal (somatosensory, spatial), temporal (auditory, memory) and occipital (visual) lobes; the insula lies deep in the lateral sulcus.
- The central sulcus separates the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) from the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex). The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
- White matter: association fibres (within a hemisphere, e.g. arcuate fasciculus), commissural fibres (between hemispheres, e.g. corpus callosum) and projection fibres (to and from lower centres, e.g. internal capsule).
- Basal ganglia: caudate and putamen (striatum), globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra.
- Thalamus relays most sensory input to the cortex; hypothalamus directs autonomic and endocrine control.
- Cranial nerve nuclei: III and IV in the midbrain; V (main sensory and motor), VI, VII and VIII in the pons; IX, X and XII in the medulla.
- Spinal cord: dorsal horn sensory, ventral horn motor, lateral horn autonomic (thoracic, upper lumbar and sacral levels). In adults the cord usually ends around L1–L2 (conus medullaris), with the cauda equina below.

Arterial supply and stroke territories
The internal carotid arteries give the anterior (ACA) and middle (MCA) cerebral arteries. The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which supplies the brainstem and cerebellum and ends as the two posterior cerebral arteries (PCA). Anterior and posterior communicating arteries complete the circle of Willis, which can partly compensate when one inflow is blocked; its anatomy varies between people.
- ACA: medial surface of the hemisphere, including the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex. Occlusion causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss affecting the leg more than face and arm.
- MCA: most of the lateral surface, including face and arm areas and, in the dominant hemisphere, language areas. Its deep lenticulostriate branches supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness more than leg, sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, and aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant).
- PCA: occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal lobe. Occlusion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
- The posterior limb of the internal capsule packs corticospinal fibres for face, arm and leg into a small area, so a small lacunar infarct there can cause a dense pure motor hemiparesis.

CSF is produced mainly by the choroid plexus in the ventricles (roughly 500 mL a day, with about 150 mL present at any time; approximate). It flows:
- lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina (of Monro) → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinuses.
The meninges are dura, arachnoid and pia. Blood can collect in different compartments: extradural (usually arterial, classically middle meningeal artery after a temporal fracture), subdural (bridging veins, often older people or after minor trauma) and subarachnoid (usually a ruptured berry aneurysm near the circle of Willis).
Obstruction within the ventricular system (e.g. aqueduct stenosis, a posterior fossa mass) causes non-communicating hydrocephalus; impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations (e.g. after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis) causes communicating hydrocephalus. Lacunar syndromes (pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor or ataxic hemiparesis) have no cortical signs. notes.overview: Sensory pathways follow a fixed pattern of receptor, first-, second- and third-order neurons, and the point where each pathway crosses the midline is what lets you localise a lesion. This topic covers touch and pain pathways, pain modulation, the visual pathway and field defects, and the tuning-fork tests used to separate types of hearing loss.
objectives: Trace the dorsal column and spinothalamic pathways and state where each crosses.
Predict the sensory findings of a spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard syndrome).
Localise a lesion from a visual field defect and explain the pupillary light reflex.
Interpret Rinne and Weber tests.
Explain gate control, descending modulation and referred pain.

sections.body:
Stimulus intensity is coded by firing rate and by how many receptors are recruited; location by which receptors fire (receptive fields).
- Rapidly adapting receptors signal change: Meissner corpuscles (light touch, flutter) and Pacinian corpuscles (vibration).
- Slowly adapting receptors signal sustained stimuli: Merkel discs (pressure, texture) and Ruffini endings (skin stretch).
- Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs provide proprioception.
- Nociceptors are free nerve endings.
Fibre types: Aβ (large, myelinated, fast) carry touch and vibration; Aδ (thinly myelinated) carry sharp, well-localised "first" pain and cold; C fibres (unmyelinated, slow) carry burning, poorly localised "second" pain and warmth.
A dermatome is the skin area supplied by one spinal root. Useful landmarks: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot and sole.

- Dorsal column–medial lemniscus (fine touch, vibration, proprioception): first-order fibres ascend on the same side in the gracile (lower body) and cuneate (upper body) fasciculi and synapse in the medulla. Second-order fibres cross there and ascend in the medial lemniscus to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus; third-order fibres project to the postcentral gyrus.
- Spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature, crude touch): first-order fibres synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order fibres cross within a segment or two in the anterior white commissure and ascend on the opposite side to the thalamus.
So a cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard) gives, below the lesion, same-side weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception, with opposite-side loss of pain and temperature starting one to two levels below.
Pain is modulated. Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965) proposed that Aβ input activates dorsal horn inhibitory interneurons, reducing nociceptive transmission (why rubbing a bump helps). Descending pathways from the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla use endogenous opioids, serotonin and noradrenaline. Referred pain arises because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same dorsal horn neurons, as in cardiac pain felt in the left arm.

Visual pathway: retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm, where fibres from the nasal half of each retina (carrying the temporal visual field) cross → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiation → primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus.
- Optic nerve lesion: loss of vision in that eye.
- Chiasm (e.g. pituitary adenoma pressing from below): bitemporal hemianopia, often upper fields first.
- Optic tract, radiation or cortex: contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Temporal lobe lesions of Meyer's loop give a contralateral upper ("pie in the sky") quadrantanopia; parietal radiation lesions classically give a lower quadrantanopia.
- Pupillary light reflex: optic nerve (afferent) → pretectal nuclei → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei → oculomotor nerve and ciliary ganglion (efferent). Bilateral connections give the consensual response.
Hearing: cochlear hair cells are tonotopic (high frequencies at the base). Tuning-fork tests (512 Hz): in conductive loss, bone conduction is louder than air on the affected side (Rinne negative) and Weber lateralises to the affected ear; in sensorineural loss, air stays louder than bone (Rinne positive) and Weber lateralises to the better ear.
Balance: semicircular canals detect angular acceleration; the utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and head tilt.

- Students often think a lesion behind the chiasm affects one eye. It affects the same half of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous).
- Students often think "Rinne negative" means normal. Rinne positive (air louder than bone) is normal; Rinne negative suggests a conductive loss in that ear.
- Students often think Weber lateralises towards the deaf ear in all hearing loss. It goes to the affected ear in conductive loss but to the better ear in sensorineural loss.
- Students often think gate control theory explains all pain modulation. It was a landmark idea, but descending control, central sensitisation and psychological factors are also important.

notes.h: Motor systems: upper and lower motor neurons, basal ganglia and cerebellum
notes.overview: Movement depends on a final common path (the lower motor neuron) shaped by descending upper motor neuron commands, the basal ganglia (which select and scale movements) and the cerebellum (which corrects errors). Recognising which level is damaged, from the pattern of signs, is the core skill of the neurological examination.
objectives: Distinguish upper from lower motor neuron signs and explain each.
Describe the stretch reflex and the roles of muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs.
Explain the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways and how dopamine loss causes bradykinesia.
Explain why cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral signs.
Apply these principles to motor neurone disease, Parkinson's disease and cerebellar disease.

sections.body:
The lower motor neuron (LMN) is the alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn or a cranial nerve nucleus, plus its axon. A motor unit is one motor neuron and the muscle fibres it supplies; small units are recruited first (Henneman's size principle).
Upper motor neurons (UMNs) start mainly in the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus). The corticospinal tract passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the cerebral peduncle, the basal pons and the medullary pyramids. Most fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract (limb muscles); the uncrossed anterior tract mainly serves trunk muscles.
- UMN lesion: weakness in a pyramidal pattern (upper limb extensors and lower limb flexors weaker), spasticity (velocity-dependent, often clasp-knife), brisk reflexes, extensor plantar response and clonus; little wasting apart from disuse.
- LMN lesion: weakness of the muscles supplied, wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone and reduced or absent reflexes.
- Straight after an acute cord or cerebral lesion, tone and reflexes may be reduced ("shock") before UMN signs appear.

Stretch reflex: stretching a muscle stretches its spindles; Ia afferents excite alpha motor neurons to the same muscle monosynaptically and, via interneurons, inhibit the antagonist (reciprocal inhibition). Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity. Golgi tendon organs sense tension (Ib afferents) and inhibit the motor neuron. Descending UMN pathways normally restrain these reflexes, which is why UMN lesions make them brisk.
Basal ganglia loops (cortex → striatum → output nuclei → thalamus → cortex):
- The output nuclei (internal globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata) tonically inhibit the thalamus.
- Direct pathway: striatal neurons with D1 receptors inhibit the output nuclei, releasing the thalamus and facilitating movement.
- Indirect pathway: striatal D2 neurons inhibit the external globus pallidus, releasing the subthalamic nucleus, which excites the output nuclei and suppresses movement.
- Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway; both effects favour movement.
Cerebellum: compares intended movement with sensory feedback and corrects errors. The vermis governs trunk and gait; the hemispheres govern limb coordination. Its output crosses to the opposite thalamus and cortex, and the corticospinal tract crosses back, so a hemisphere lesion causes same-side signs.

- Parkinsonism (basal ganglia): bradykinesia (slowness with decrement on repetition), rigidity (lead-pipe, or cogwheel with tremor; not velocity-dependent), rest tremor, and later postural instability.
- Chorea (e.g. Huntington's disease, with early loss of indirect-pathway striatal neurons) and hemiballismus (contralateral subthalamic nucleus lesion) are hyperkinetic.
- Cerebellar signs (DANISH): dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred (scanning) speech and hypotonia or heel–shin ataxia. Vermis lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia; hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia on the same side.
- Romberg's test is positive when balance fails with the eyes closed: it tests proprioceptive (sensory) ataxia, not cerebellar function.
- Mixed UMN and LMN signs in the same limbs, with no sensory loss and normal eye movements, suggest motor neurone disease.

A 64-year-old has six months of weakness of the right hand, difficulty turning keys and, recently, slurred speech. There is wasting of the small hand muscles, fasciculation in the forearms and thighs, brisk biceps and knee reflexes and extensor plantars. Sensation is normal.
- Wasting and fasciculation are LMN signs; brisk reflexes and extensor plantars are UMN signs. Finding both in the same regions, without sensory signs, is the hallmark of motor neurone disease.
- Important differentials include cervical myelopathy with radiculopathy (often with neck pain and sensory signs) and multifocal motor neuropathy (LMN only).
- Neurophysiology (EMG and nerve conduction) supports the diagnosis; care is multidisciplinary, and breathing is monitored because respiratory muscle weakness develops (NICE NG42 recommends non-invasive ventilation where appropriate).
By contrast, a patient whose hand is slow to open and close, with fatigue of amplitude on repeated tapping, rigidity and a rest tremor, has parkinsonism; and a patient whose finger overshoots the target with tremor that worsens as the target nears has a cerebellar lesion on that side.

- Students often expect cerebellar lesions to cause signs on the opposite side, like cortical lesions. Hemisphere lesions cause same-side signs because the pathway crosses twice.

- Students often think dopamine only excites movement pathways. It excites the direct pathway (D1) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D2); both effects facilitate movement.

notes.overview: The autonomic nervous system controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands through two-neuron chains. Knowing where each division leaves the CNS, which transmitter and receptor act at each step, and how reflexes such as the baroreflex work explains Horner's syndrome, postural hypotension and the effects of many drugs and poisons.
objectives: Compare the anatomy of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
State the transmitter and receptor at each autonomic synapse, including the important exceptions.
Explain the baroreceptor reflex and why its failure causes postural hypotension.
Localise Horner's syndrome along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway.
Predict the effects of anticholinergic and cholinergic drugs and toxins.

sections.body:
Both divisions use a preganglionic neuron in the CNS and a postganglionic neuron in a peripheral ganglion.
Sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow:
- Preganglionic cell bodies lie in the lateral horn of the thoracic and upper lumbar cord (classically T1–L2).
- Axons leave in the ventral roots and white rami and synapse in the paravertebral chain ganglia or, via splanchnic nerves, in prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric).
- Postganglionic fibres rejoin spinal nerves through grey rami to reach skin and vessels. Preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres long.
- The adrenal medulla is a modified ganglion: preganglionic fibres reach it directly and its chromaffin cells release mainly adrenaline into the blood.
Parasympathetic (craniosacral) outflow:
- Cranial nerves III (ciliary ganglion: pupil constriction and accommodation), VII (pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia: lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands), IX (otic ganglion: parotid) and X (thoracic and abdominal viscera).
- Sacral cord (classically S2–S4) via pelvic splanchnic nerves: hindgut, bladder and erectile tissue.
- Ganglia lie in or near target organs, so preganglionic fibres are long.
The hypothalamus and brainstem centres (such as the nucleus tractus solitarius) coordinate autonomic output.

- All preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors in the ganglia (and the adrenal medulla).
- Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors (M2 in the heart slows rate; M3 on smooth muscle and glands).
- Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline onto adrenoceptors: α₁ (Gq: vasoconstriction, pupil dilation), α₂ (Gi: presynaptic inhibition of release), β₁ (Gs: faster heart rate and stronger contraction, renin release) and β₂ (Gs: bronchodilation, some vasodilation).
- Exceptions: sympathetic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
Many organs receive both divisions (dual innervation), but blood vessels are under sympathetic tone with little parasympathetic input.
The baroreceptor reflex: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (afferents in IX) and aortic arch (afferents in X) signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius. A rise in blood pressure increases vagal output and reduces sympathetic output, slowing the heart and dilating vessels; a fall does the opposite. On standing, about half a litre of blood pools in the legs and the baroreflex normally restores pressure within seconds.

- Horner's syndrome: interruption of the sympathetic supply to the eye causes partial ptosis (superior tarsal muscle), miosis and sometimes anhidrosis, on the same side. The pathway has three neurons: hypothalamus to the T1 lateral horn (first order; e.g. lateral medullary stroke, MS, syringomyelia), T1 through the chain to the superior cervical ganglion (second order; e.g. Pancoast tumour at the lung apex), and along the internal carotid artery to the eye (third order; e.g. carotid dissection, cavernous sinus lesions). Postganglionic lesions tend not to cause facial anhidrosis.
- Third nerve palsy, by contrast, causes a dilated pupil with complete ptosis and an eye that rests down and out.
- Autonomic failure (e.g. diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy) causes postural hypotension without a compensatory rise in heart rate, erectile dysfunction, bladder and bowel disturbance, and abnormal sweating.
- Anticholinergic toxicity: hot dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds and agitation or delirium.
- Cholinergic excess (e.g. organophosphates): increased secretions, sweating, small pupils, bradycardia, bronchospasm and muscle fasciculation then weakness (nicotinic effects).

A simple bedside test of autonomic cardiovascular reflexes is lying and standing blood pressure.
- Measure blood pressure and pulse after the patient has been lying for a few minutes, then again after standing for at least one minute (and ideally again at three minutes).
- NICE NG136 defines postural hypotension as a fall in systolic blood pressure of 20 mmHg or more, or a fall in diastolic pressure of 10 mmHg or more, on standing (with or without symptoms).

notes.h: Higher functions: cortex, language, memory and executive function
notes.overview: Higher functions such as language, memory, attention and social behaviour depend on distributed cortical networks, but damage to particular regions still produces recognisable syndromes. This topic links lobes to functions, sets out the aphasias, memory systems and frontal syndromes, and shows how to localise a cognitive deficit at the bedside.

Distinguish Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction and global aphasia by fluency, comprehension and repetition.

- Frontal lobe: primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), premotor and supplementary motor areas, frontal eye fields, Broca's area (posterior inferior frontal gyrus, dominant hemisphere) and prefrontal cortex. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex supports working memory, planning and set-shifting; the orbitofrontal and ventromedial regions support social behaviour, inhibition and decision-making.
- Parietal lobe: primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus). The dominant parietal lobe supports language, calculation, writing and praxis; the non-dominant parietal lobe supports spatial attention and body awareness.
- Temporal lobe: auditory cortex, Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, dominant), hippocampus and entorhinal cortex (declarative memory), amygdala (emotion and fear learning) and the ventral "what" visual stream.
- Occipital lobe: primary visual cortex and association areas, including regions specialised for colour and motion.
Language is left-dominant in most right-handed people and in most left-handed people. Split-brain studies after corpus callosotomy (Sperry and Gazzaniga) showed that information presented only to the right hemisphere could not be named aloud, demonstrating left-hemisphere dominance for speech.

Aphasia is a disorder of language. Classify it by fluency, comprehension and repetition:
- Broca's (expressive): non-fluent, effortful, telegraphic speech; comprehension relatively good (complex grammar can be hard); repetition impaired; patients are usually aware and frustrated.
- Wernicke's (receptive): fluent but empty speech with paraphasias and neologisms; poor comprehension; impaired repetition; insight often poor.
- Conduction: fluent speech with paraphasias, good comprehension but disproportionately impaired repetition (lesion near the supramarginal gyrus or arcuate fasciculus).
- Global: all domains impaired, usually after a large dominant MCA stroke.
- Transcortical aphasias spare repetition.
Memory:
- Declarative (explicit) memory covers episodic (events) and semantic (facts) memory and depends on the medial temporal lobe (hippocampus and entorhinal cortex) for forming new memories.
- Non-declarative (implicit) memory includes procedural skills and habits (striatum), classical conditioning (cerebellum for motor responses, amygdala for emotional responses) and priming.
- Working memory (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974) has a central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad; the episodic buffer was added in 2000.

- Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) had bilateral medial temporal lobe removal to treat severe seizures. He could no longer form new declarative memories (anterograde amnesia), yet improved at mirror drawing across days without remembering doing it, showing that procedural memory uses a separate system.
- Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome follows thiamine deficiency (often with alcohol misuse or malnutrition). - Dorsolateral prefrontal damage: apathy, poor planning and set-shifting (dysexecutive syndrome). Orbitofrontal damage: disinhibition, impulsivity and socially inappropriate behaviour, as in Phineas Gage (1848) and behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia.
- Non-dominant (usually right) parietal damage: hemispatial neglect of the left side, often with anosognosia (denial of deficit).

notes.overview: Most drugs acting on the nervous system change one step of synaptic transmission: synthesis, storage, release, receptor activation, reuptake or breakdown. Knowing the main transmitter systems lets you predict both the intended effects and the adverse effects of antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiparkinsonian drugs, sedatives, opioids and antiepileptic drugs. No doses are given here.
objectives: Explain how drugs modify GABA and glutamate transmission, including benzodiazepines and NMDA antagonists.
Relate the four dopamine pathways to the therapeutic and adverse effects of antipsychotics.
Explain the mechanisms of the main antidepressant classes and why tricyclics are dangerous in overdose.
Recognise serotonin syndrome and anticholinergic toxicity from their mechanisms.
Summarise current UK safety measures for valproate.

sections.body:
- Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter, acting on ionotropic AMPA, NMDA and kainate receptors and on metabotropic receptors. Ketamine and memantine block NMDA receptors.
- GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain. GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated Cl⁻ channels; GABA-B receptors are G-protein coupled (baclofen, used for spasticity, is a GABA-B agonist).
- Benzodiazepines bind at the interface of the α and γ subunits of the GABA-A receptor and mainly increase how often the channel opens when GABA is present; they do not open it on their own. Barbiturates prolong channel opening and at high concentrations can open it directly, which is one reason they are more dangerous in overdose.
- Combining sedatives (benzodiazepines, alcohol, opioids, gabapentinoids) adds respiratory depression.
- Opioids act on μ (and δ, κ) receptors, which are Gi/o coupled: they inhibit adenylyl cyclase, open K⁺ channels and close presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels. Effects include analgesia, respiratory depression, miosis, nausea and constipation. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist.

Dopamine has four main pathways:
- nigrostriatal (movement), mesolimbic (reward; overactivity linked to positive psychotic symptoms), mesocortical (cognition and motivation; underactivity linked to negative symptoms) and tuberoinfundibular (dopamine inhibits prolactin release).
- Antipsychotics block D2 receptors: mesolimbic blockade reduces positive symptoms; nigrostriatal blockade causes extrapyramidal effects (parkinsonism, acute dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia); tuberoinfundibular blockade raises prolactin. Many newer ("atypical") drugs also block 5-HT2A receptors.
- Parkinson's drugs replace or mimic dopamine: levodopa (given with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor), dopamine agonists, and MAO-B and COMT inhibitors that slow breakdown.
Serotonin and noradrenaline:
- SSRIs block the serotonin transporter; SNRIs also block the noradrenaline transporter. Reuptake block is immediate but mood benefit takes weeks, implying slower adaptive changes.
- Tricyclics block serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake but also muscarinic, H1 and α₁ receptors and cardiac Na⁺ channels.
- MAO inhibitors prevent monoamine breakdown; dietary tyramine can then cause a hypertensive crisis.
Acetylcholine: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) boost cholinergic transmission in dementia; pyridostigmine acts peripherally in myasthenia gravis.

- Serotonin syndrome (excess serotonergic activity, often from combining drugs such as an SSRI with tramadol, an MAOI, linezolid or MDMA): altered mental state, autonomic instability (fever, sweating, tachycardia, diarrhoea) and neuromuscular hyperactivity (tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, especially inducible or ocular). The Hunter criteria rely on clonus and related signs after exposure to a serotonergic drug. Management is to stop the drugs and give supportive care, with senior input for severe cases.
- Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (dopamine blockade or sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs): fever, severe "lead-pipe" rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability and a very high creatine kinase; it usually develops over days and reflexes are not brisk.
- Tricyclic overdose: anticholinergic features, seizures, hypotension and a broad QRS from Na⁺ channel blockade, which predicts arrhythmias.
- Opioid toxicity: reduced consciousness, slow shallow breathing and pinpoint pupils.
- Anticholinergic toxicity: hot dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention and delirium.

These are high-level safety principles only; no doses are given.

- NICE NG97 recommends the three acetylcholinesterase inhibitors as options for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, with memantine as an option in some situations, and donepezil or rivastigmine for mild to moderate dementia with Lewy bodies.
- NICE NG71 says people starting dopamine agonists must be told about the increased risk of impulse control disorders (such as pathological gambling or hypersexuality).

- Students often think antidepressants work as soon as reuptake is blocked. Transporter blockade is immediate but mood benefit takes weeks.
- Students often think extrapyramidal side effects come from the drug acting on the mesolimbic pathway. They come from nigrostriatal D2 blockade; raised prolactin comes from the tuberoinfundibular pathway.
- Students often treat serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome as the same. Serotonin syndrome is rapid with hyperreflexia and clonus; NMS evolves over days with rigidity and reduced reflexes.
- Students often think memantine is a cholinesterase inhibitor. It is an NMDA receptor antagonist.

notes.h: Common neurological disorders: stroke, epilepsy, Parkinson's, MS, dementia, headache and neuromuscular disease
notes.overview: This topic applies the neuroscience of the pack to the neurological conditions most often met on wards and in the UK Medical Licensing Assessment. For each, link the mechanism to the presentation, know which test answers which question, and know the current UK guidance principles for the first hours of care.
objectives: Explain the mechanisms behind stroke, seizures, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and the main dementias.
Recognise red-flag presentations: acute stroke, thunderclap headache, status epilepticus and suspected meningitis.
Interpret CSF results and choose the right first investigation for each presentation.
Apply current NICE principles for TIA, acute ischaemic stroke, first seizure, status epilepticus and suspected Parkinson's disease.
Distinguish Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis and motor neurone disease.

sections.body:
- Stroke: a sudden focal deficit of vascular cause, mostly ischaemic. A TIA resolves fully.
- Epilepsy: an enduring tendency to unprovoked seizures. The ILAE 2017 classification sorts seizures by onset (focal, generalised or unknown); focal seizures are aware or impaired awareness.
- Parkinson's disease: loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with α-synuclein Lewy bodies.
- Multiple sclerosis: immune-mediated CNS demyelination, typically in young adults and more often women.
- Dementias: Alzheimer's (amyloid plaques, tau tangles, early hippocampal involvement), vascular, Lewy body and frontotemporal.
- Neuromuscular: Guillain–Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory polyneuropathy, often after infection), myasthenia gravis (antibodies against acetylcholine receptors, or MuSK, at the neuromuscular junction) and motor neurone disease (degeneration of UMNs and LMNs).

- Ischaemic stroke: an occlusion creates a core of irreversible infarction surrounded by a penumbra of underperfused but salvageable tissue. Rapid reperfusion aims to save the penumbra ("time is brain").
- Seizures: excessive, hypersynchronous firing from an imbalance of excitation (glutamate) and inhibition (GABA).
- Parkinson's disease: striatal dopamine loss increases thalamic inhibition (bradykinesia); non-motor features (reduced smell, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation) can come years earlier.
- MS: plaques of demyelination slow or block conduction; lesions are separated in space and time.
- Guillain–Barré syndrome: antibodies triggered by an infection (Campylobacter jejuni is a classic trigger) attack peripheral nerve myelin or axons.
- Myasthenia gravis: fewer functional postsynaptic receptors, so the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission fails with repeated use (fatigability).

- Parkinson's disease: asymmetric bradykinesia with rest tremor and/or rigidity. Early falls, early dementia, symmetrical onset or poor levodopa response suggest an atypical parkinsonian syndrome.
- MS: optic neuritis (painful visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect), sensory symptoms, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, transverse myelitis.
- Dementia with Lewy bodies: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics.
- Guillain–Barré syndrome: ascending weakness and tingling from feet and hands, areflexia, and risk of respiratory failure.
- Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ptosis, diplopia and bulbar or limb weakness; normal reflexes and sensation.
- Headache red flags: thunderclap onset (subarachnoid haemorrhage), fever with neck stiffness or rash (meningitis), papilloedema or headache worse lying down (raised pressure), new headache after 50 with jaw claudication (giant cell arteritis), new focal deficit, cancer or immunosuppression.

- Suspected stroke: urgent non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage (immediately if thrombolysis or thrombectomy might be given, or if the patient takes anticoagulants or has a bleeding tendency), with CT angiography when thrombectomy is being considered. Check capillary glucose: hypoglycaemia mimics stroke.
- Thunderclap headache: urgent non-contrast CT; CT is most accurate within 6 hours of onset. If CT is negative and was done more than 6 hours after onset, consider lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset, with spectrophotometry for bilirubin (xanthochromia).
- Suspected meningitis: lumbar puncture without prior imaging unless there is a contraindication such as signs of raised intracranial pressure. Typical bacterial CSF: neutrophils, high protein, CSF:blood glucose ratio below 0.5. Viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose ratio.
- Guillain–Barré syndrome: CSF protein raised with a normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation), nerve conduction studies, and serial spirometry (FVC).
- MS: MRI of brain and spinal cord; CSF oligoclonal bands (or kappa free light chains in the 2024 McDonald criteria) support the diagnosis.
- Myasthenia: acetylcholine receptor antibodies (MuSK if negative) and CT thorax for thymoma.

- TIA (NICE NG128): give aspirin immediately unless contraindicated and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset; do not use risk scores such as ABCD2 to decide urgency.
- Acute ischaemic stroke (NG128): once haemorrhage is excluded, thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) within 4.5 hours of onset if there are no contraindications; thrombectomy as soon as possible within 6 hours for proximal anterior circulation occlusion, from 6 to 24 hours if imaging shows salvageable brain, and considered up to 24 hours for basilar or posterior cerebral artery occlusion; aspirin as soon as possible and within 24 hours once haemorrhage is excluded; keep blood glucose 4–11 mmol/L.
- Epilepsy (NG217): refer urgently after a first suspected seizure (seen within 2 weeks). Convulsive status epilepticus (seizures lasting 5 minutes or more) is treated first with a benzodiazepine.
- Parkinson's disease (NG71): refer quickly and untreated to a specialist; diagnose clinically using the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria; do not use structural MRI to diagnose it.
- MS: the 2024 McDonald criteria (published 2025) add the optic nerve as a fifth site; after a June 2026 surveillance review NICE is updating NG220 to refer to them.

A 29-year-old woman had painful blurred vision in her right eye last year that recovered over weeks. She now has numbness of both legs rising to the waist. Her symptoms briefly worsen after a hot bath. Examination shows a right relative afferent pupillary defect, brisk leg reflexes and a sensory level.
- Two episodes affecting different parts of the CNS (optic nerve, then spinal cord) separated in time is the pattern of MS.
- Heat sensitivity (Uhthoff's phenomenon) reflects fragile conduction in demyelinated axons.
- MRI of brain and spinal cord is the key investigation, looking for lesions disseminated in space and time; CSF oligoclonal bands support it. A sensory level also prompts exclusion of cord compression.

- Students often think ABCD2 scores should triage TIA. NICE NG128 advises against using them; everyone with a suspected TIA is seen within 24 hours.

- Students often think lumbar puncture is done straight away for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage. It waits at least 12 hours so bilirubin can form, and only follows a negative CT done after 6 hours.

cards.f: Why does the resting membrane potential lie close to E_K?
cards.b: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to other ions, so K⁺ diffusion dominates. A small Na⁺ leak keeps it slightly less negative than E_K.
cards.ex: The ion with the highest permeability pulls the membrane potential towards its own equilibrium potential.

cards.f: Calculate E_K if [K⁺]out = 5 mM and [K⁺]in = 140 mM (37 °C).
cards.ex: Use outside over inside; a ratio below 1 gives a negative log, so E_K is negative.

cards.f: What causes the absolute refractory period?
cards.b: Inactivation of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels: they cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises and the inactivation gate resets. This makes conduction one-way and limits firing rate.
cards.ex: It is channel inactivation, not hyperpolarisation, that prevents a second spike.

cards.f: How does myelin increase conduction velocity?
cards.b: It raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current spreads further along the axon; the action potential is regenerated only at nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction).
cards.ex: Less charge leaks out and less is needed to charge the membrane, so the depolarisation reaches the next node quickly.

cards.f: What triggers neurotransmitter release?
cards.b: Depolarisation of the terminal opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin and SNARE proteins fuse vesicles with the membrane (exocytosis).
cards.ex: Remove extracellular Ca²⁺ and the action potential still arrives, but release fails.

cards.f: Ionotropic versus metabotropic receptors
cards.b: Ionotropic: ligand-gated channels, fast (ms), e.g. nicotinic, AMPA, GABA-A. Metabotropic: G-protein coupled, slower and longer-lasting, e.g. muscarinic, GABA-B, D2.
cards.ex: Ask whether the receptor is itself a pore (ionotropic) or acts through a G protein (metabotropic).

cards.f: Three conditions for an NMDA receptor to conduct
cards.b: Glutamate bound, co-agonist glycine (or D-serine) bound, and depolarisation to expel the Mg²⁺ block. It then admits Ca²⁺ as well as Na⁺.
cards.ex: Needing both presynaptic release and postsynaptic depolarisation makes it a coincidence detector.

cards.f: Why can severe hyperkalaemia reduce excitability even though it depolarises cells?
cards.b: Sustained depolarisation keeps many voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivated, so fewer are available to fire an action potential.
cards.ex: Depolarised is not the same as excitable: channels must recover from inactivation to fire.

cards.f: A patient has descending flaccid paralysis after eating home-preserved food. What is the synaptic mechanism?
cards.b: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins in cholinergic terminals, blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction (and autonomic synapses).
cards.ex: The fault is presynaptic release, not the receptor (contrast myasthenia gravis).

cards.f: Spatial versus temporal summation
cards.b: Spatial: EPSPs from different synapses arriving together add up. Temporal: repeated EPSPs from one synapse arrive before the previous one decays. Both are integrated at the initial segment.
cards.ex: Spatial = many places; temporal = one place, many times.

cards.f: Who first described long-term potentiation, and where?
cards.b: Bliss and Lømo (1973), in the dentate gyrus of the rabbit hippocampus after high-frequency stimulation of the perforant path.
cards.ex: LTP was found in the hippocampus, the structure linked to declarative memory by patient H.M.

cards.f: Precentral versus postcentral gyrus
cards.b: Precentral gyrus (frontal lobe): primary motor cortex. Postcentral gyrus (parietal lobe): primary somatosensory cortex. The central sulcus lies between them.
cards.ex: Pre = in front of the central sulcus = motor.

cards.f: Why does an anterior cerebral artery occlusion cause leg-predominant weakness?
cards.b: The leg area of the motor and sensory cortex lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere, which the ACA supplies.
cards.ex: Picture the homunculus draped over the top of the hemisphere with the leg hanging down the medial side.

cards.f: What does the middle cerebral artery supply?
cards.b: Most of the lateral hemisphere (face and arm motor and sensory areas; language areas on the dominant side) plus the basal ganglia and internal capsule via lenticulostriate branches.
cards.ex: MCA = lateral surface + deep lenticulostriates.

cards.f: Trace CSF from production to absorption.
cards.b: Choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinuses.
cards.ex: Learn the two narrow points (foramina and aqueduct), where blockage causes non-communicating hydrocephalus.

cards.f: Communicating versus non-communicating hydrocephalus
cards.b: Non-communicating: CSF flow blocked within the ventricles (e.g. aqueduct stenosis). Communicating: flow out of the ventricles is free but absorption is impaired (e.g. after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis).
cards.ex: "Communicating" means the ventricles still communicate with the subarachnoid space.

cards.f: Why can a small lacunar infarct in the internal capsule cause a dense hemiparesis?
cards.b: Corticospinal fibres for face, arm and leg are packed tightly into the posterior limb, so a small lesion interrupts all of them.
cards.ex: Compare the cortex (spread out) with the capsule (bundled).

cards.f: Which cranial nerve nuclei lie in the midbrain, pons and medulla?
cards.b: Midbrain: III, IV. Pons: V (main sensory and motor), VI, VII, VIII. Medulla: IX, X, XII (XI largely from the upper cervical cord).
cards.ex: Rule of 2s: 2 above the pons (I, II), 2 in midbrain, 4 in pons, 4 in medulla/cord.

cards.f: Sudden left leg weakness with little arm or face involvement. Which artery?
cards.b: Right anterior cerebral artery: the leg area lies on the medial surface of the right hemisphere, controlling the left side.
cards.ex: Contralateral, and leg-predominant means ACA.

cards.f: A stroke patient has right face and arm weakness, right homonymous hemianopia and dysphasia. Oxford classification?
cards.b: Total anterior circulation syndrome: unilateral weakness of two of face/arm/leg, homonymous hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction are all present (left MCA territory).
cards.ex: TACS needs all three; any two is a PACS.

cards.f: Why is macular sparing common in posterior cerebral artery stroke?
cards.b: The occipital pole, which represents the macula, often receives collateral supply from the MCA, and the macula has a large cortical representation.
cards.ex: Dual supply at the occipital pole protects central vision.

cards.f: Extradural versus subdural haematoma
cards.b: Extradural: usually arterial (middle meningeal) after skull fracture, biconvex, can deteriorate fast after a lucid interval. Subdural: torn bridging veins, crescentic, often older people or anticoagulated, may be slow.
cards.ex: Extra = outside the dura, against the bone, limited by sutures (lens shape).

cards.f: Where do dorsal column fibres cross?
cards.b: In the medulla, after synapsing in the gracile and cuneate nuclei; second-order fibres cross as internal arcuate fibres and ascend in the medial lemniscus.
cards.ex: Dorsal columns stay on the same side throughout the cord.

cards.f: Dorsal column versus spinothalamic pathway
cards.b: Dorsal column: fine touch, vibration, proprioception; crosses in the medulla. Spinothalamic: pain, temperature, crude touch; crosses within one or two segments of entry in the cord.
cards.ex: This difference is what makes a hemisection give split findings on the two sides.

cards.f: Right cord hemisection at T10: predict the sensory and motor findings.
cards.b: Below the lesion: right UMN weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception; left loss of pain and temperature starting one to two levels below.
cards.ex: Ask on which side each tract runs at the level of the lesion.

cards.f: Bitemporal hemianopia: where is the lesion?
cards.b: At the optic chiasm, where fibres from the nasal retinas (temporal fields) cross; classically compression by a pituitary adenoma, often upper fields first.
cards.ex: Crossing fibres carry the temporal fields of both eyes.

cards.f: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"): where is the lesion?
cards.b: Left temporal lobe, affecting Meyer's loop of the optic radiation, which carries the upper visual field.
cards.ex: Temporal = upper; parietal = lower; contralateral to the field loss.

cards.f: Rinne negative on the left (bone louder than air) and Weber lateralises to the left.
cards.b: Left conductive hearing loss, e.g. wax, otitis media or otosclerosis.
cards.ex: In conductive loss Weber goes to the bad ear.

cards.f: Rinne positive both sides, Weber lateralises to the right.
cards.b: Left sensorineural hearing loss: air remains louder than bone, and Weber is heard in the better (right) ear.
cards.ex: In sensorineural loss Weber goes to the good ear.

cards.f: Outline gate control theory of pain.
cards.b: Melzack and Wall (1965): large Aβ touch fibres activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that reduce transmission from Aδ and C nociceptors to projection neurons.
cards.ex: It explains why rubbing a painful area brings some relief.

cards.f: Why is cardiac pain often felt in the left arm?
cards.b: Visceral afferents from the heart and somatic afferents from the arm converge on the same dorsal horn neurons (around T1–T4), so the brain misattributes the source (referred pain).
cards.ex: Convergence onto shared second-order neurons.

cards.f: Aδ versus C fibres
cards.b: Aδ: thinly myelinated, faster, sharp well-localised first pain and cold. C: unmyelinated, slow, burning poorly localised second pain and warmth.
cards.ex: Myelin = speed = sharp first pain.

cards.f: Why does a central cord lesion (syrinx) cause cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch?
cards.b: It damages spinothalamic fibres crossing in the anterior white commissure at those levels, while dorsal columns (touch, vibration) are spared.
cards.ex: Crossing fibres sit next to the central canal.

cards.f: UMN versus LMN signs
cards.b: UMN: pyramidal weakness, spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar, clonus, little wasting. LMN: wasting, fasciculation, low tone, reduced or absent reflexes.
cards.ex: Ask whether the reflex arc is intact but unrestrained (UMN) or broken (LMN).

cards.f: Where does the corticospinal tract decussate?
cards.b: At the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla; most fibres cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract, the rest descend uncrossed in the anterior tract.
cards.ex: Below the medulla, a cord lesion gives same-side UMN weakness.

cards.f: Describe the stretch reflex circuit.
cards.b: Spindle stretch excites Ia afferents, which synapse directly on alpha motor neurons of the same muscle and, via interneurons, inhibit the antagonist (reciprocal inhibition).
cards.ex: Monosynaptic excitation plus disynaptic inhibition of the antagonist.

cards.f: Why are reflexes brisk after a UMN lesion?
cards.b: Descending pathways normally restrain spinal reflex circuits and gamma drive; when they are lost, the intact reflex arc becomes overactive.
cards.ex: The arc is intact but unrestrained.

cards.f: How does dopamine affect the direct and indirect pathways?
cards.b: It excites direct-pathway neurons via D1 receptors and inhibits indirect-pathway neurons via D2 receptors. Both reduce output-nucleus inhibition of the thalamus and facilitate movement.
cards.ex: Two receptor types, one net effect: more movement.

cards.f: Why does nigral dopamine loss cause bradykinesia?
cards.b: Less D1 drive weakens the direct pathway and less D2 inhibition strengthens the indirect pathway, so GPi/SNr inhibit the thalamus more and cortical motor drive falls.
cards.ex: More output-nucleus inhibition = less thalamic support for movement.

cards.f: Which lesion causes hemiballismus?
cards.b: A lesion (often a small infarct) of the subthalamic nucleus on the side opposite the flailing limbs.
cards.ex: Loss of the indirect pathway's excitatory drive releases movement.

cards.f: Why do cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral signs?
cards.b: Cerebellar output crosses to the opposite thalamus and motor cortex, and the corticospinal tract crosses back, so the deficit is on the same side as the lesion.
cards.ex: Two crossings cancel out.

cards.f: Spasticity versus rigidity
cards.b: Spasticity (UMN): velocity-dependent, clasp-knife, greatest in certain muscle groups. Rigidity (extrapyramidal): constant through the range in all directions, lead-pipe or cogwheel.
cards.ex: Move the limb faster: spasticity increases, rigidity does not.

cards.f: Wasting and fasciculation in the hands with brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, normal sensation. Interpretation?
cards.b: Mixed UMN and LMN signs without sensory loss suggest motor neurone disease (differential: cervical myelopathy with radiculopathy).
cards.ex: MND is the classic cause of UMN and LMN signs together.

cards.f: Vermis versus hemisphere cerebellar lesions
cards.b: Vermis: truncal and gait ataxia (e.g. alcohol), limbs relatively spared. Hemisphere: ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia.
cards.ex: Midline controls the trunk; lateral controls the limbs.

cards.f: Where are sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies?
cards.b: Sympathetic: lateral horn of thoracic and upper lumbar cord (T1–L2). Parasympathetic: brainstem nuclei of III, VII, IX and X and the sacral cord (S2–S4).
cards.ex: Thoracolumbar versus craniosacral.

cards.f: Which transmitter and receptor operate in all autonomic ganglia?
cards.b: Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors (neuronal type), in both divisions and at the adrenal medulla.
cards.ex: Ganglionic transmission is always cholinergic nicotinic.

cards.f: Why do anticholinergic drugs cause hot, dry skin?
cards.b: Sweat glands are supplied by sympathetic but cholinergic (muscarinic) fibres; blocking muscarinic receptors stops sweating, so heat cannot be lost and skin is hot and dry.
cards.ex: The sweat gland exception explains "dry as a bone".

cards.f: Describe the baroreflex response to standing up.
cards.b: Blood pools in the legs, carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch falls, afferent firing (IX, X) to the NTS falls, vagal output drops and sympathetic output rises: heart rate, contractility and vascular tone increase.
cards.ex: Less stretch → less vagal brake and more sympathetic drive.

cards.f: Horner's syndrome versus third nerve palsy (eye findings)
cards.b: Horner's: partial ptosis, small pupil (miosis), eye movements normal. Third nerve palsy: complete ptosis, dilated pupil (if compressive), eye down and out.
cards.ex: Sympathetic loss = small pupil; parasympathetic (III) loss = big pupil.

cards.f: Left Horner's syndrome with facial anhidrosis and arm pain in a heavy smoker. Likely level?
cards.b: Second-order (preganglionic) lesion at the lung apex, e.g. a Pancoast tumour; needs urgent chest imaging.
cards.ex: Anhidrosis plus apical symptoms point to a preganglionic lesion.

cards.f: Why is the small pupil of Horner's syndrome most obvious in dim light?
cards.b: In dim light the normal pupil dilates through sympathetic action, but the affected pupil cannot, so the size difference (anisocoria) increases.
cards.ex: Sympathetic failure shows up when dilation is needed.

cards.f: Lying BP 132/78, standing at 3 minutes 104/70, heart rate 72 to 74. Interpretation?
cards.b: Systolic fall of 28 mmHg (≥20) meets the NICE definition of postural hypotension; the lack of heart-rate rise suggests autonomic (neurogenic) failure.
cards.ex: Look at the heart rate response, not just the BP fall.

cards.f: A farmer exposed to an organophosphate has pinpoint pupils, sweating, drooling, bradycardia and wheeze. Mechanism?
cards.b: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic (secretions, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm) and nicotinic synapses (fasciculation, then weakness).
cards.ex: Too much ACh everywhere it acts.

cards.f: α₁ versus β₂ adrenoceptor effects
cards.b: α₁ (Gq): vasoconstriction, pupil dilation, sphincter contraction. β₂ (Gs): bronchodilation, some vasodilation (e.g. skeletal muscle), uterine relaxation.
cards.ex: Same transmitter, opposite effects on smooth muscle depending on receptor.

cards.f: Why is the adrenal medulla called a modified sympathetic ganglion?
cards.b: Its chromaffin cells come from neural crest, receive preganglionic cholinergic fibres directly and release adrenaline (and some noradrenaline) into the blood instead of across a synapse.
cards.ex: It is the postganglionic neuron turned endocrine cell.

cards.f: Broca's versus Wernicke's aphasia
cards.b: Broca's: non-fluent, effortful, comprehension relatively good, repetition impaired, inferior frontal gyrus. Wernicke's: fluent with paraphasias, poor comprehension, repetition impaired, posterior superior temporal gyrus.
cards.ex: Fluency and comprehension separate them; repetition is impaired in both.

cards.f: Fluent speech, good comprehension, but cannot repeat a sentence. Which aphasia?
cards.b: Conduction aphasia, classically from damage near the supramarginal gyrus or arcuate fasciculus.
cards.ex: Disproportionate repetition failure is the hallmark.

cards.f: What did patient H.M. reveal about memory?
cards.b: After bilateral medial temporal lobe removal he could not form new declarative memories but still learned mirror drawing, showing declarative and procedural memory use different systems.
cards.ex: He improved at a skill he could not remember practising.

cards.f: Components of Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model
cards.b: Central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad (1974), with the episodic buffer added in 2000.
cards.ex: Two slave systems plus an executive, then a buffer.

cards.f: A patient ignores the left side of the page and denies any weakness. Likely lesion?
cards.b: Right (non-dominant) parietal lobe: hemispatial neglect of the left side with anosognosia.
cards.ex: Neglect is classically a non-dominant parietal sign.

cards.f: Which structures are damaged in Korsakoff syndrome, and why?
cards.b: Mammillary bodies and medial (dorsomedial) thalamus, from thiamine deficiency, often in alcohol misuse; it causes severe amnesia with confabulation.
cards.ex: Thiamine deficiency → diencephalic memory circuit damage.

cards.f: Dorsolateral prefrontal versus orbitofrontal syndrome
cards.b: Dorsolateral: apathy, poor planning, working memory and set-shifting (dysexecutive). Orbitofrontal: disinhibition, impulsivity and socially inappropriate behaviour.
cards.ex: Dorsolateral = thinking; orbital = behaving.

cards.f: Aphasia versus dysarthria
cards.b: Aphasia: disorder of language (word choice, grammar, comprehension). Dysarthria: disorder of articulation from weakness or incoordination of speech muscles; language is intact (writing and comprehension normal).
cards.ex: Ask the patient to write: written language is impaired in aphasia but not dysarthria.

cards.f: Why can a split-brain patient not name an object shown only in the left visual field?
cards.b: The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere; without the corpus callosum the information cannot reach the left hemisphere, which controls speech in most people.
cards.ex: Visual fields cross; language is usually left.

cards.f: A 45-year-old becomes rude, disinhibited and overeats sweet food over two years, with little concern. Memory and navigation are fairly preserved. Likely diagnosis?
cards.b: Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (orbitofrontal and anterior temporal involvement).
cards.ex: Early personality change with relatively spared memory points frontal.

cards.f: Declarative versus non-declarative memory
cards.b: Declarative (explicit): episodic and semantic, medial temporal lobe. Non-declarative (implicit): skills and habits (striatum), conditioning (cerebellum, amygdala), priming.
cards.ex: Can the person consciously report it? Then declarative.

cards.f: Benzodiazepines versus barbiturates at the GABA-A receptor
cards.b: Benzodiazepines mainly increase opening frequency and need GABA present. Barbiturates prolong opening and can open the channel directly at high concentrations, so overdose is more dangerous.
cards.ex: Modulator versus potential direct agonist.

cards.f: Name the four dopamine pathways and the effect of D2 blockade in each.
cards.b: Mesolimbic: fewer positive symptoms. Mesocortical: may worsen negative and cognitive symptoms. Nigrostriatal: extrapyramidal effects. Tuberoinfundibular: raised prolactin.
cards.ex: One drug action, four places, four effects.

cards.f: Why is levodopa given with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor?
cards.b: The inhibitor (e.g. carbidopa) does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it stops levodopa being converted to dopamine in the periphery: more reaches the brain and peripheral effects such as nausea fall.
cards.ex: Block conversion outside the brain, not inside.

cards.f: Why are tricyclic antidepressants dangerous in overdose?
cards.b: Besides reuptake block, they block cardiac Na⁺ channels (broad QRS, arrhythmias), muscarinic receptors (anticholinergic toxicity) and α₁ receptors (hypotension), and can cause seizures.
cards.ex: Na⁺ channel block is what kills.

cards.f: Cellular mechanism of μ-opioid agonists
cards.b: Through Gi/o they inhibit adenylyl cyclase, open K⁺ channels (hyperpolarisation) and close presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels (less transmitter release).
cards.ex: Inhibitory G-protein coupling at both sides of the synapse.

cards.f: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
cards.b: Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset after serotonergic drugs; tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, dilated pupils. NMS: develops over days after dopamine blockade; severe rigidity, reduced reflexes, very high CK.
cards.ex: Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin; lead-pipe rigidity to NMS.

cards.f: What does memantine do, and when is it used?
cards.b: An NMDA receptor antagonist, used as an option in Alzheimer's disease (e.g. moderate disease when cholinesterase inhibitors are unsuitable, or severe disease).
cards.ex: Memantine is glutamatergic, not cholinergic.

cards.f: Key MHRA safety rule for starting valproate
cards.b: In anyone under 55, two specialists must independently consider and document the decision; anyone who could become pregnant must follow the pregnancy prevention programme.
cards.ex: Teratogenicity drives the restrictions; check the latest MHRA update.

cards.f: A man taking an antipsychotic develops parkinsonism. Why is adding levodopa not the usual answer?
cards.b: The parkinsonism results from nigrostriatal D2 blockade; levodopa would oppose the D2 blockade the antipsychotic relies on and could worsen psychosis. Review the antipsychotic instead.
cards.ex: Treat the cause: the dopamine blockade.

cards.f: Why do antidepressants take weeks to improve mood when reuptake block is immediate?
cards.b: The delay suggests that benefit depends on slower adaptive changes (receptor regulation, gene expression, neuroplasticity) rather than on the rise in synaptic monoamine itself.
cards.ex: Immediate pharmacology, delayed adaptation.

cards.f: A patient on an MAO inhibitor eats mature cheese and develops a severe headache and very high blood pressure. Mechanism?
cards.b: Dietary tyramine, normally broken down by gut and liver MAO, enters the circulation and releases noradrenaline from sympathetic nerves, causing a hypertensive crisis.
cards.ex: MAO normally protects us from dietary amines.

cards.f: NICE NG128 time window for thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke
cards.b: Within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (tenecteplase or alteplase), once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded and there are no contraindications.
cards.ex: Haemorrhage must be excluded first: CT before thrombolysis.

cards.f: Suspected TIA that has fully resolved. What does NICE NG128 advise?
cards.b: Aspirin immediately unless contraindicated, and specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset; do not use ABCD2 or similar scores to decide urgency.
cards.ex: Everyone is urgent; scores are not used for triage.

cards.f: What is the ischaemic penumbra and why does it matter?
cards.b: Underperfused but still viable tissue around the infarct core. Restoring flow quickly (thrombolysis, thrombectomy) can save it, hence "time is brain".
cards.ex: Core is lost; penumbra is the target of treatment.

cards.f: How does NICE define convulsive status epilepticus, and what is first-line treatment?
cards.b: Seizures lasting 5 minutes or more (or repeated without recovery); first-line treatment is a benzodiazepine.
cards.ex: Treat at 5 minutes, not 30.

cards.f: CSF: protein 1.6 g/L, white cells 2 ×10⁶/L, glucose ratio normal, in a patient with ascending weakness and areflexia.
cards.b: Albuminocytological dissociation (high protein, normal cell count) supports Guillain–Barré syndrome.
cards.ex: High protein without cells is the GBS pattern.

cards.f: Bacterial versus viral meningitis CSF
cards.b: Bacterial: neutrophils, raised protein, CSF:blood glucose ratio below 0.5. Viral: lymphocytes, raised protein (often mild), normal glucose ratio.
cards.ex: Bacteria consume glucose; viruses usually do not lower it.

cards.f: Why is lumbar puncture for suspected SAH delayed until at least 12 hours after onset?
cards.b: Red cells in CSF need time to break down to bilirubin; xanthochromia detected by spectrophotometry distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap.
cards.ex: Bilirubin takes hours to form.

cards.f: Why do MS symptoms worsen in a hot bath (Uhthoff's phenomenon)?
cards.b: Demyelinated axons have a low safety margin for conduction; warmth speeds Na⁺ channel inactivation and further reduces it, so conduction blocks temporarily.
cards.ex: Heat tips marginal conduction into block.

cards.f: Guillain–Barré syndrome versus myasthenia gravis
cards.b: GBS: progressive ascending weakness, areflexia, sensory symptoms, high CSF protein. Myasthenia: fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia), normal reflexes and sensation, AChR or MuSK antibodies.
cards.ex: Reflexes and fatigability separate them.

cards.f: A 67-year-old has asymmetric rest tremor and bradykinesia. What does NICE NG71 advise before starting treatment?
cards.b: Refer quickly and untreated to a specialist in Parkinson's disease, who diagnoses clinically using the UK Brain Bank criteria.
cards.ex: Untreated referral keeps the diagnosis clear.

cards.f: Features suggesting dementia with Lewy bodies
cards.b: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder; severe sensitivity to antipsychotics.
cards.ex: Fluctuation plus hallucinations plus parkinsonism.

questions.q: Which ion movement is mainly responsible for the rising (depolarising) phase of a neuronal action potential?
questions.why: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open at threshold and Na⁺ rushes in down its electrochemical gradient, driving the membrane towards E_Na. The opening is self-reinforcing, which is why the upstroke is rapid and all-or-none.
optWhy: Cl⁻ influx makes the inside more negative or clamps it near rest; it is inhibitory.
Correct: Na⁺ entry through voltage-gated channels drives the rising phase towards E_Na.
Ca²⁺ moves into cells, not out, when its channels open; in axons it is not the main depolarising ion (it triggers release at terminals).
K⁺ efflux through delayed voltage-gated K⁺ channels causes repolarisation, not the upstroke.
questions.clue: The "rising (depolarising) phase" of a neuronal action potential.
questions.concept: Ionic basis of the action potential.

followUp.q: A toxin binds and blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in an axon (as tetrodotoxin does). What happens to action potentials?
options: They are unaffected because K⁺ carries the upstroke
They last longer because repolarisation is delayed
followUp.why: Without Na⁺ current there is no regenerative upstroke, so action potentials are not generated (the resting potential is largely unchanged because it depends mainly on K⁺). Delayed repolarisation would come from blocking K⁺ channels, and K⁺ does not carry the neuronal upstroke.

questions.q: A neuron has [Na⁺] 145 mM outside and 15 mM inside. Using E ≈ 61.5 log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV at 37 °C, what is E_Na closest to?
questions.why: Ratio = 145/15 ≈ 9.7; log₁₀(9.7) ≈ 0.985; 61.5 × 0.985 ≈ +61 mV. The ratio is above 1, so the equilibrium potential for a cation that is concentrated outside is positive.
optWhy: −61 mV inverts the ratio (inside over outside), giving the wrong sign.
+75 mV would need a ratio of about 16.5, not 9.7.
+90 mV would need a ratio of about 29; it may come from confusing the size of E_Na with that of E_K (about −89 mV).
+40 mV is roughly the peak of a real action potential, which stays below E_Na because K⁺ channels open and Na⁺ channels inactivate.
Correct: 61.5 × log₁₀(9.7) ≈ +61 mV.
questions.clue: Concentrations 145 mM outside and 15 mM inside, and the simplified Nernst equation.
questions.concept: Applying the Nernst equation.

followUp.q: If extracellular K⁺ rises from 4 mM to 8 mM (intracellular 140 mM), how does E_K change?
options: It becomes about 18 mV more negative
It becomes about 18 mV less negative
followUp.why: E_K changes by 61.5 × log₁₀(2) ≈ 18.5 mV for a doubling of [K⁺]out, becoming less negative (about −95 mV to about −76 mV). Doubling a concentration changes the log term additively, not the potential twofold. This depolarisation is the basis of the cardiac and neuromuscular effects of hyperkalaemia.

questions.q: A 70-year-old with acute kidney injury has a serum potassium of 7.2 mmol/L. His ECG shows peaked T waves and broadening QRS complexes, and he reports muscle weakness. Which best explains why excitable tissue becomes LESS able to fire despite being depolarised?
options: Cl⁻ conductance rises, clamping cells at rest
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels remain inactivated by sustained depolarisation
E_K becomes more negative, hyperpolarising cells
Acetylcholine release fails at the neuromuscular junction
