questions.why: Raised extracellular K⁺ makes E_K and the resting potential less negative. Sustained depolarisation closes the inactivation gates of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so fewer channels are available; conduction slows (broad QRS) and weakness follows.
optWhy: No change in Cl⁻ conductance is implied; this describes shunting inhibition at GABA-A synapses.
Pump failure is not the explanation; the change arises from the altered K⁺ gradient, and the pump contributes only a few millivolts directly.
Correct: inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot open, so excitability falls despite depolarisation.
Raising extracellular K⁺ makes E_K less negative, not more.
Hyperkalaemia does not primarily block transmitter release; the weakness reflects muscle membrane depolarisation.
questions.clue: Serum potassium 7.2 mmol/L, broad QRS and weakness "despite being depolarised".
questions.concept: Depolarisation inactivates Na⁺ channels and reduces excitability.

followUp.q: Why does lowering extracellular Ca²⁺ (hypocalcaemia) make nerves MORE excitable, causing tingling and tetany?
options: Less extracellular Ca²⁺ lowers the threshold for Na⁺ channel opening
Low Ca²⁺ hyperpolarises the resting membrane
Low Ca²⁺ blocks K⁺ channels and prolongs action potentials
Ca²⁺ is needed for vesicle release, so less Ca²⁺ increases release
followUp.why: Extracellular Ca²⁺ stabilises the membrane by screening surface charge near Na⁺ channels; when it falls, Na⁺ channels open at less depolarised voltages, so nerves fire spontaneously. Lower Ca²⁺ would reduce, not increase, transmitter release, and it does not hyperpolarise the membrane.

questions.q: A researcher applies a drug that blocks NMDA receptors to hippocampal slices. Baseline synaptic responses are unchanged, but high-frequency stimulation no longer produces long-term potentiation. Which property of NMDA receptors best explains this?
options: They admit Ca²⁺ only when glutamate binding coincides with postsynaptic depolarisation
They are found only on presynaptic terminals
They are blocked by GABA at rest
They are metabotropic and act through cAMP
They mediate most of the baseline fast EPSP
questions.why: NMDA receptors pass current only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised enough to expel Mg²⁺. During high-frequency input this coincidence occurs and Ca²⁺ enters, triggering LTP. Baseline transmission is carried mainly by AMPA receptors, which is why it is unaffected.
optWhy: Correct: the Mg²⁺ block makes NMDA receptors coincidence detectors whose Ca²⁺ entry induces LTP.
The relevant NMDA receptors are postsynaptic.
The resting block of NMDA receptors is by Mg²⁺, not GABA.
NMDA receptors are ionotropic (ligand-gated channels), not G-protein coupled.
Baseline fast EPSPs are carried mainly by AMPA receptors; that is why blocking NMDA receptors left them unchanged.
questions.clue: Baseline responses unchanged but LTP abolished by NMDA blockade.
questions.concept: NMDA receptors as coincidence detectors for LTP.

followUp.q: In rats, infusing an NMDA receptor antagonist into the brain impairs learning of a hidden-platform location in a water maze. What does this result support?
options: That spatial memory is stored in the cerebellum
That AMPA receptors are not needed for transmission
That LTP is irrelevant to learning
That NMDA-dependent plasticity contributes to spatial learning
followUp.why: Morris and colleagues (1986) found that the NMDA antagonist AP5 impaired spatial learning at doses that blocked hippocampal LTP, linking NMDA-dependent plasticity to learning. It does not prove LTP is the memory mechanism, and it says nothing about the cerebellum or about AMPA receptors.

questions.q: Explain how a chemical synapse transmits a signal, from arrival of the action potential to termination of transmitter action.
markScheme: Action potential depolarises the terminal and opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin; SNARE proteins fuse vesicles; transmitter released by exocytosis
Transmitter binds ionotropic (fast) or metabotropic (slow, G-protein) receptors
Produces EPSP or IPSP; summation (spatial/temporal) at the initial segment decides firing
Action ends by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) or diffusion
questions.modelAnswer: When the action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal it depolarises the membrane and opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Ca²⁺ enters and binds synaptotagmin, and SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin on the vesicle, syntaxin and SNAP-25 on the membrane) pull docked vesicles into the membrane so transmitter is released by exocytosis. Transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels that produce fast responses (for example AMPA or nicotinic receptors); metabotropic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers, producing slower, longer-lasting effects. Depending on the ions involved the result is an EPSP, moving the membrane towards threshold, or an IPSP, moving it away. These potentials sum spatially and temporally, and if the initial segment reaches threshold the postsynaptic neuron fires. Transmission ends when transmitter is taken back up (glutamate, GABA, monoamines), broken down (acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase) or diffuses away.
questions.concept: Sequence of chemical synaptic transmission.

questions.q: A 66-year-old develops sudden weakness of the right leg, with mild right arm weakness and no facial weakness or language disturbance. Occlusion of which artery best explains this?
questions.why: Leg-predominant weakness points to the anterior cerebral artery, because the leg area lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere. Motor pathways cross, so right-sided weakness means a left hemisphere lesion.
optWhy: The left PCA would mainly cause a right homonymous hemianopia, not leg weakness.
Basilar occlusion typically causes brainstem signs, bilateral deficits or reduced consciousness.
The left MCA would affect the right face and arm more than the leg and, in the dominant hemisphere, cause dysphasia.
Correct: left ACA territory includes the medial motor cortex controlling the right leg.
The right ACA would cause left leg weakness.
questions.clue: Weakness "of the right leg" with milder arm and no face or language involvement.
questions.concept: ACA territory and contralateral control.

followUp.q: A patient has a right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and no weakness. Which artery is most likely occluded?
followUp.why: An isolated homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing, is typical of occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the opposite occipital lobe. The right PCA would give a left hemianopia; the left MCA would usually add face and arm weakness and dysphasia; the ACA does not supply visual cortex.

questions.q: A 78-year-old has sudden left face, arm and leg weakness, a left homonymous hemianopia and ignores the left side of space. Using the Oxford (Bamford) classification, how is this stroke classified?
questions.why: All three criteria are present: unilateral weakness of at least two of face, arm and leg; homonymous hemianopia; and higher cortical dysfunction (neglect, a visuospatial disorder). That defines a total anterior circulation syndrome, here in the right MCA territory.
optWhy: A partial anterior circulation syndrome has only two of the three criteria (or higher cortical dysfunction alone).
Correct: weakness, hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction together make a TACS.
Posterior circulation syndromes include isolated hemianopia, cerebellar or brainstem signs, not this full anterior picture.
A TIA resolves; this is an established deficit described as a stroke.
A lacunar syndrome has no cortical signs such as neglect or hemianopia.
questions.clue: Weakness of face, arm and leg plus hemianopia plus neglect.
questions.concept: Oxford (Bamford) stroke classification.

followUp.q: A 70-year-old has pure weakness of the right face, arm and leg, with no sensory loss, visual field defect or cognitive or language problem. Which syndrome is this?
followUp.why: Pure motor stroke without cortical signs is a lacunar syndrome, typically from a small vessel infarct in the internal capsule or pons. TACS and PACS need hemianopia or higher cortical dysfunction; posterior syndromes have brainstem, cerebellar or isolated visual signs.

questions.q: Through which structure does CSF pass from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle?
questions.why: The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain and connects the third and fourth ventricles. It is narrow, so stenosis there causes non-communicating hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral and third ventricles but a normal fourth ventricle.
optWhy: The median aperture lets CSF leave the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.
The central canal continues down the spinal cord from the fourth ventricle and carries little flow.
Arachnoid granulations absorb CSF into the dural venous sinuses.
The interventricular foramina connect the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle.
Correct: the cerebral aqueduct links the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.clue: "From the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle".
questions.concept: CSF pathway anatomy.

followUp.q: A CT scan shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles but a normal-sized fourth ventricle. Where is the obstruction most likely?
options: At the median and lateral apertures
followUp.why: Dilatation stops at the third ventricle, so the block lies between the third and fourth ventricles: the cerebral aqueduct. Blocking the apertures would also enlarge the fourth ventricle; impaired absorption at the granulations or sinuses typically enlarges all four ventricles (communicating hydrocephalus).

questions.q: Three weeks after a subarachnoid haemorrhage, a 52-year-old becomes increasingly drowsy and has urinary incontinence and an unsteady gait. CT shows enlargement of all four ventricles. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Impaired CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
Overproduction of CSF by a choroid plexus tumour
Brain atrophy with compensatory ventricular enlargement
questions.why: Blood in the subarachnoid space can impair CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations, causing communicating hydrocephalus in which all four ventricles enlarge. The timing after SAH and the new symptoms fit this.
optWhy: An extradural haematoma follows trauma and would appear as a lens-shaped collection, not ventricular enlargement alone.
Aqueduct stenosis would spare the fourth ventricle.
Correct: after SAH, impaired absorption causes communicating hydrocephalus with all ventricles enlarged.
Choroid plexus tumours are rare and usually seen in children; there is a clear alternative cause here.
Atrophy develops slowly and would not explain a subacute deterioration after SAH.
questions.clue: "Three weeks after a subarachnoid haemorrhage" with all four ventricles enlarged.
questions.concept: Communicating versus non-communicating hydrocephalus.

followUp.q: A child has a mass in the posterior fossa compressing the fourth ventricle. Which type of hydrocephalus would you expect?
options: No hydrocephalus, because CSF is absorbed in the ventricles
Hydrocephalus confined to the spinal canal
Communicating hydrocephalus with all ventricles enlarged equally
followUp.why: A mass obstructing the fourth ventricle blocks flow within the ventricular system, causing non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus with dilated ventricles upstream. Communicating hydrocephalus is from impaired absorption; CSF is absorbed at the arachnoid granulations, not in the ventricles.

questions.q: Describe the arterial supply of the cerebral hemispheres and predict the main deficit from occlusion of each cerebral artery.
markScheme: Internal carotids → ACA and MCA; vertebrals → basilar → PCAs; circle of Willis via communicating arteries
ACA: medial surface incl. leg area → contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss
MCA: lateral surface (face/arm, language on dominant side) and lenticulostriates to internal capsule → contralateral face/arm weakness, sensory loss, hemianopia, aphasia or neglect
PCA: occipital and inferomedial temporal lobe → contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often macular sparing
Notes variability of collaterals and the dense effect of small internal capsule (lacunar) lesions
questions.modelAnswer:
Each internal carotid artery divides into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which supplies the brainstem and cerebellum and ends as the two posterior cerebral arteries. The anterior and posterior communicating arteries link these into the circle of Willis, which can provide collateral flow, although its anatomy varies.

The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of motor and sensory cortex, so occlusion causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss affecting the leg more than the arm and face. The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral surface, including the face and arm areas and, in the dominant hemisphere, the language areas; its lenticulostriate branches supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss, a homonymous hemianopia, and aphasia (dominant side) or neglect (non-dominant side). The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal lobe, so occlusion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing. Small deep infarcts in lenticulostriate territory can cause a dense pure motor hemiparesis because fibres are tightly packed in the internal capsule.
questions.concept: Cerebral arterial territories and stroke localisation.

questions.q: A 55-year-old says she keeps bumping into objects on her right. Confrontation testing shows loss of the upper right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
questions.why: A homonymous defect in both eyes means a lesion behind the chiasm on the opposite side. Fibres for the upper field loop forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop), so a left temporal lesion gives a right upper quadrantanopia.
optWhy: Correct: Meyer's loop in the left temporal lobe carries the right upper field.
Left parietal radiation lesions classically cause a right lower quadrantanopia.
A right occipital lesion causes a left-sided field defect.
An optic nerve lesion affects one eye only.
A chiasmal lesion typically causes bitemporal (not homonymous) loss.
questions.clue: Loss of the "upper right quadrant" in both eyes.
questions.concept: Localising lesions of the visual pathway.

followUp.q: A 45-year-old has headaches and has stopped noticing cars on both sides when driving. Fields show loss of the outer (temporal) half of the field in each eye, worse above. Which lesion fits best?
options: A pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm from below
followUp.why: Bitemporal hemianopia, worse in the upper fields, is typical of a pituitary adenoma pressing on the crossing nasal fibres from below. Occipital and temporal lesions give homonymous defects; optic neuritis causes central visual loss in the affected eye.

questions.q: After a stab wound to the back, a 28-year-old has left leg weakness with an extensor plantar, loss of vibration and joint position sense in the left leg, and loss of pain and temperature in the right leg from just below the umbilicus. What is the lesion?
options: Right hemisection of the spinal cord at about T10
Left hemisection of the spinal cord at about T8–T9
questions.why: Same-side weakness and dorsal column loss with opposite-side spinothalamic loss is Brown-Séquard syndrome. The weakness and dorsal column loss are on the left, so the lesion is on the left. Spinothalamic loss begins one to two segments below the lesion, and the umbilicus is T10, so the cord lesion is around T8–T9.
optWhy: Central cord syndrome mainly affects the arms, with cape-like sensory loss.
A radiculopathy causes LMN weakness and dermatomal sensory loss, not UMN signs and crossed findings.
A right hemisection would give right-sided weakness and right-sided proprioceptive loss.
Correct: a left hemisection, with the level one to two segments above the upper limit of the contralateral pain loss.
Anterior spinal artery infarction causes bilateral weakness and pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal columns.
questions.clue: Weakness and proprioceptive loss on the left; pain and temperature loss on the right below the umbilicus.
questions.concept: Brown-Séquard syndrome localisation.

followUp.q: A patient has bilateral leg weakness and bilateral loss of pain and temperature below T6, but vibration and joint position sense are normal. Which lesion fits best?
followUp.why: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) but not the dorsal columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries. Posterior column disease spares pain and temperature; a hemisection gives unilateral weakness; a peripheral neuropathy is length-dependent and lacks a sensory level.

questions.q: Which sensory modality is carried mainly in the spinothalamic tract?
questions.why: The spinothalamic (anterolateral) tract carries pain, temperature and crude touch. Its second-order fibres cross within one or two segments of entry.
optWhy: Joint position sense (proprioception) is carried in the dorsal columns.
Correct: pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract.
Two-point discrimination (fine touch) uses the dorsal columns.
Spindle stretch information travels in Ia afferents to the cord and to the cerebellum, not the spinothalamic tract.
Vibration is carried in the dorsal columns.
questions.clue: "Mainly in the spinothalamic tract".
questions.concept: Modalities carried by each ascending pathway.

followUp.q: A patient with long-standing vitamin B12 deficiency has an ataxic gait that worsens with the eyes closed, and reduced vibration sense in the feet. Which pathway is mainly affected?
followUp.why: B12 deficiency can damage the dorsal columns (subacute combined degeneration), causing loss of vibration and proprioception and a sensory ataxia that worsens without vision (positive Romberg's test). The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; corticospinal damage causes weakness and UMN signs.

questions.q: A 40-year-old has gradual hearing loss in the right ear. With a 512 Hz fork, Rinne's test on the right is negative (bone louder than air) and Weber's test lateralises to the right. What is the most likely type of hearing loss?
questions.why: In conductive loss, sound conducted through bone bypasses the faulty middle ear, so bone beats air (Rinne negative) on that side, and Weber is heard louder in the affected ear because ambient noise is masked there.
optWhy: Left conductive loss would send Weber to the left.
A negative Rinne with lateralised Weber is not normal.
Right sensorineural loss would keep air louder than bone on the right and send Weber to the left.
Left sensorineural loss would send Weber to the right but leave the right Rinne positive.
Correct: Rinne negative on the right and Weber to the right indicate right conductive loss.
questions.clue: Right Rinne negative and Weber lateralising to the right.
questions.concept: Interpreting Rinne and Weber tests.

followUp.q: A 60-year-old has left-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Rinne is positive in both ears and Weber lateralises to the right. Which is most likely?
followUp.why: Air louder than bone in both ears rules out a significant conductive loss; Weber going to the better (right) ear indicates a left sensorineural loss, which with unilateral tinnitus warrants investigation (for example for a vestibular schwannoma). Conductive losses send Weber to the affected ear.

questions.q: A patient's left pupil constricts only weakly when light is shone into the left eye but constricts briskly when light is shone into the right eye. When the torch swings from right to left, both pupils dilate. Explain the anatomy of this finding and how it differs from a left third nerve palsy.
markScheme: Light reflex: optic nerve afferent → pretectal nuclei → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei → III/ciliary ganglion efferent
Bilateral pretectal–Edinger–Westphal connections give a consensual response
Finding = left relative afferent pupillary defect: reduced afferent signal from the left optic nerve (e.g. optic neuritis)
Swinging to the left eye the total afferent drive falls, so both pupils dilate equally
Third nerve palsy: efferent defect; left pupil is dilated and reacts poorly whichever eye is lit, with ptosis and eye deviated down and out
questions.modelAnswer:
The pupillary light reflex has an afferent limb in the optic nerve and tract, which projects to the pretectal nuclei. Each pretectal nucleus connects with both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, and parasympathetic fibres travel in each oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion and sphincter pupillae. Because of these bilateral connections, light in one eye normally constricts both pupils equally (direct and consensual responses).

Here light in the left eye produces a weak response but light in the right eye produces a brisk one, and on swinging from right to left both pupils dilate. This is a left relative afferent pupillary defect: the left optic nerve carries less signal, so when the light moves to the left eye the total drive to the Edinger–Westphal nuclei falls and both pupils relax. The efferent pathways are intact, so the pupils remain equal in size. A common cause is optic neuritis.

In a left third nerve palsy the defect is efferent. The left pupil is larger and reacts poorly whether light is shone in the left or right eye, while the right pupil constricts normally to light in either eye. There is usually also ptosis and an eye that rests down and out.
questions.concept: Afferent versus efferent defects of the pupillary light reflex.

questions.q: Which finding indicates an upper motor neuron lesion rather than a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: Flaccid tone with absent reflexes in a single myotome
questions.why: An extensor plantar (Babinski) response indicates corticospinal tract dysfunction. Fasciculation, early wasting, hyporeflexia and segmental flaccidity are LMN features.
optWhy: Fasciculation is spontaneous firing of motor units from a diseased LMN.
Marked early wasting reflects loss of LMN trophic supply; UMN lesions cause only disuse atrophy.
Correct: an extensor plantar response is a sign of a UMN (corticospinal) lesion.
Hyporeflexia reflects interruption of the reflex arc (LMN or sensory).
Flaccidity and areflexia in one myotome indicate a root or nerve (LMN) lesion.
questions.clue: "Rather than a lower motor neuron lesion".
questions.concept: UMN versus LMN signs.

followUp.q: A 45-year-old has weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension on the right, with low tone and no reflex change. Which lesion is most likely?
options: Right L5 root or common peroneal nerve lesion
followUp.why: Focal weakness of dorsiflexion and big toe extension with low tone is an LMN pattern of L5 or common peroneal (fibular) nerve territory (inversion helps tell them apart: weak in L5, preserved in peroneal palsy). Capsular infarcts and myelopathy cause UMN signs; cerebellar lesions cause incoordination, not focal weakness.

questions.q: A 68-year-old has slowly progressive slowness, with movements becoming smaller on repeated finger tapping, rigidity of the left arm and a left hand tremor at rest. Which change in basal ganglia circuitry best explains his slowness?
options: Increased inhibitory output from the internal globus pallidus to the thalamus
Loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex
Degeneration of corticospinal neurons in the motor cortex
Excess dopamine release in the striatum
questions.why: In Parkinson's disease, loss of nigral dopamine weakens the direct pathway and strengthens the indirect pathway (including the subthalamic drive). Both increase inhibitory output from the GPi/SNr to the thalamus, reducing cortical motor drive and causing bradykinesia.
optWhy: Correct: increased GPi/SNr inhibition of the thalamus underlies bradykinesia.
Purkinje cell loss causes cerebellar ataxia, not bradykinesia with rest tremor.
Corticospinal degeneration causes UMN signs such as spasticity and extensor plantars.
Reduced subthalamic activity would decrease output-nucleus inhibition and cause hyperkinesia (hemiballismus); in PD the subthalamic nucleus is overactive.
Parkinson's disease is a loss, not an excess, of striatal dopamine.
questions.clue: Decrement on finger tapping, rigidity and rest tremor.
questions.concept: Basal ganglia circuitry in Parkinson's disease.

followUp.q: A 75-year-old with diabetes develops sudden wild flinging movements of the right arm and leg. Where is the lesion most likely?
followUp.why: Hemiballismus results from a lesion, often a small infarct, of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus; losing its excitatory drive to the output nuclei releases the thalamus. A right-sided lesion would affect the left limbs; cerebellar lesions cause ataxia; nigral loss causes parkinsonism.

questions.q: A 50-year-old with heavy alcohol use has an unsteady wide-based gait and cannot walk heel-to-toe, but finger–nose and heel–shin testing are near normal. Which part of the cerebellum is mainly affected?
questions.why: Truncal and gait ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination indicates a midline (vermis) lesion; alcohol characteristically affects the anterior superior vermis.
optWhy: Flocculonodular lesions mainly cause vestibular features such as nystagmus and imbalance; alcoholic degeneration typically involves the anterior vermis.
A right hemisphere lesion would cause right limb ataxia on finger–nose or heel–shin testing.
A left hemisphere lesion would cause left limb ataxia.
Correct: midline vermis damage causes truncal and gait ataxia with limbs relatively spared.
The dentate nucleus mainly serves the lateral hemisphere and limb coordination.
questions.clue: Wide-based gait with near-normal limb testing in heavy alcohol use.
questions.concept: Vermis versus hemisphere cerebellar lesions.

followUp.q: A 32-year-old with multiple sclerosis has intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia of the left hand and past-pointing on the left. Where is the lesion?
followUp.why: Limb ataxia is on the same side as a cerebellar hemisphere lesion because cerebellar output crosses and the corticospinal tract crosses back. A right cerebellar lesion would affect the right limbs; capsular and cortical lesions cause weakness, not intention tremor.

questions.q: A 61-year-old has a year of progressive weakness. Examination shows wasting and fasciculation of both hands and the tongue, brisk reflexes in all limbs and extensor plantars. Sensation and eye movements are normal, and there is no bladder disturbance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Combined UMN and LMN signs in several regions (including the tongue) with normal sensation and eye movements and no early sphincter disturbance is the classic picture of motor neurone disease.
optWhy: A peripheral neuropathy causes LMN signs with sensory loss and reduced reflexes.
Correct: mixed UMN and LMN signs without sensory or eye-movement involvement.
Guillain–Barré syndrome causes rapidly progressive weakness with areflexia, not brisk reflexes.
MS causes UMN and sensory signs and often eye-movement problems, but not widespread wasting and fasciculation.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and no wasting or fasciculation early on.
questions.clue: Wasting and fasciculation plus brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, with normal sensation.
questions.concept: Recognising mixed UMN and LMN signs.

followUp.q: A 55-year-old has neck pain, clumsy hands with wasting of the small hand muscles, brisk leg reflexes, extensor plantars and reduced pinprick in both hands. Which diagnosis should be considered first?
followUp.why: Mixed UMN (legs) and LMN (hands) signs with neck pain and sensory loss point to cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy, a treatable mimic of MND; MND does not cause sensory loss. Parkinson's and cerebellar disease do not cause wasting or UMN signs.

questions.q: Explain why Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, using the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia.
markScheme: Output nuclei (GPi/SNr) tonically inhibit motor thalamus
Direct pathway (D1): striatum inhibits GPi/SNr → disinhibits thalamus → facilitates movement
Indirect pathway (D2): striatum inhibits GPe → STN released → excites GPi/SNr → suppresses movement
Dopamine from SNc excites D1 and inhibits D2 neurons; loss of SNc neurons removes both effects
Net increase in GPi/SNr inhibition of thalamus → less cortical drive → bradykinesia
questions.modelAnswer: The basal ganglia act through loops from cortex to striatum, then to the output nuclei (internal globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata), then to the motor thalamus and back to cortex. The output nuclei are inhibitory and tonically suppress the thalamus. In the direct pathway, striatal neurons with D1 receptors inhibit the output nuclei, releasing the thalamus and facilitating movement. In the indirect pathway, striatal neurons with D2 receptors inhibit the external globus pallidus; this releases the subthalamic nucleus, which excites the output nuclei and suppresses movement. Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites direct-pathway neurons and inhibits indirect-pathway neurons, so normally it facilitates movement through both routes. In Parkinson's disease these dopaminergic neurons degenerate. The direct pathway is under-active and the indirect pathway (including the subthalamic nucleus) is over-active, so output-nucleus inhibition of the thalamus rises. Thalamocortical drive falls, movements are hard to start and become small and slow (bradykinesia).
questions.concept: Basal ganglia circuit model of parkinsonian bradykinesia.

questions.q: A 52-year-old has a drooping right upper eyelid. The right pupil is smaller than the left, especially in a dim room, and both react to light. Eye movements are full. Which pathway is affected?
questions.why: Partial ptosis with a small pupil on the same side, more obvious in dim light, and full eye movements is Horner's syndrome from interruption of the right sympathetic supply to the eye.
optWhy: A left-sided sympathetic lesion would make the left pupil smaller.
An optic nerve lesion causes an afferent pupillary defect with equal pupil sizes, not ptosis.
The facial nerve closes the eye; its palsy causes inability to close the eye, not ptosis.
Loss of oculomotor parasympathetic fibres would cause a dilated pupil, usually with ptosis and impaired eye movements.
Correct: right Horner's syndrome (partial ptosis, miosis, anisocoria worse in the dark).
questions.clue: Partial right ptosis with a smaller right pupil, worse in dim light, and full eye movements.
questions.concept: Horner's syndrome versus third nerve palsy.

followUp.q: A 60-year-old has a complete left ptosis; lifting the lid shows the left eye deviated down and out with a large, unreactive pupil. What is the lesion?
options: Left third nerve palsy, possibly compressive
followUp.why: Complete ptosis, a down-and-out eye and a dilated pupil indicate a left oculomotor nerve palsy; pupil involvement raises concern about compression (for example by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm). Horner's causes a small pupil and partial ptosis; a sixth nerve palsy causes failure of abduction without ptosis.

questions.q: Which receptor mediates the sympathetic increase in heart rate?
questions.why: Noradrenaline acting on β₁ receptors (Gs, raising cAMP) in the sinoatrial node increases heart rate and in the myocardium increases contractility.
optWhy: α₁ receptors mainly mediate vasoconstriction.
α₂ receptors are mostly presynaptic and reduce noradrenaline release.
Correct: β₁ receptors increase heart rate and contractility.
M2 receptors mediate vagal slowing of the heart.
Nicotinic receptors are in autonomic ganglia, not the sinoatrial node effector cells.
questions.clue: "Sympathetic increase in heart rate".
questions.concept: Autonomic receptor subtypes and their effects.

followUp.q: A patient with severe sinus bradycardia from excessive vagal activity is given atropine. Which receptor does atropine block to increase heart rate?
followUp.why: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist; blocking M2 receptors in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes removes the vagal brake. It does not act on adrenoceptors, and it has little effect at nicotinic ganglionic receptors.

questions.q: A 23-year-old is brought in confused after taking an unknown quantity of a tricyclic antidepressant. He is hot and flushed with dry skin, dilated pupils, a heart rate of 128/min, a palpable bladder and absent bowel sounds. Which receptor blockade explains most of these features?
questions.why: This is an anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) syndrome: blocking muscarinic receptors causes dry skin (sweat glands), mydriasis, tachycardia (loss of vagal tone), urinary retention, reduced gut motility and delirium. Tricyclics also block sodium channels, which causes their dangerous cardiac effects.
optWhy: Correct: muscarinic blockade produces the anticholinergic toxidrome.
Nicotinic stimulation would cause fasciculation and autonomic ganglionic effects, not this toxidrome.
α₂ stimulation reduces sympathetic outflow and would cause sedation and bradycardia, with small pupils.
D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal effects and raised prolactin, not this picture.
β-blockade would slow the heart and would not cause dry skin or urinary retention.
questions.clue: Hot, dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils, tachycardia and urinary retention.
questions.concept: Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) toxicity.

followUp.q: A 45-year-old farmer collapses after spraying crops. He has small pupils, profuse sweating and salivation, wheeze, bradycardia and muscle twitching. What is the mechanism?
followUp.why: Organophosphate pesticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic synapses (secretions, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm) and nicotinic synapses (fasciculation, later weakness). Muscarinic blockade gives the opposite picture; β₂ stimulation would cause bronchodilation; blocking release (as with botulinum) causes weakness without secretions.

questions.q: A 72-year-old with long-standing type 2 diabetes reports dizziness on standing. Lying blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg with a pulse of 76/min; after three minutes standing it is 112/72 mmHg with a pulse of 78/min. Which interpretation is best?
options: Normal response: a small fall is expected
Postural hypotension with an inadequate heart-rate response, suggesting autonomic neuropathy
Postural hypotension due to dehydration, with an appropriate tachycardia
questions.why: Systolic falls by 30 mmHg (142 to 112), which meets the NICE NG136 threshold (systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more). The pulse barely changes, so the baroreflex fails to increase heart rate, which fits diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Medicines should also be reviewed.
optWhy: Vasovagal syncope involves sudden bradycardia and hypotension with a trigger and prodrome, not a sustained postural fall.
The issue is a fall on standing; intensifying antihypertensives could worsen it.
A 30 mmHg systolic fall is not a normal response.
Correct: significant postural drop with no compensatory heart-rate rise suggests neurogenic failure.
Dehydration would typically produce a clear compensatory tachycardia.
questions.clue: Systolic fall from 142 to 112 mmHg with pulse 76 to 78/min in diabetes.
questions.concept: Baroreflex failure and the definition of postural hypotension.

followUp.q: A 30-year-old with three days of vomiting has a lying BP of 118/76 mmHg (pulse 88/min) and standing BP of 96/70 mmHg (pulse 122/min). What does the heart-rate response suggest?
options: An intact baroreflex responding to volume depletion
followUp.why: The systolic fall of 22 mmHg meets the postural hypotension threshold, and the large rise in heart rate shows the baroreflex is working, compensating for reduced circulating volume. Autonomic failure would give little heart-rate change; complete heart block causes a fixed slow rate.

questions.q: Compare the anatomical organisation and neurotransmitters of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
markScheme: Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (T1–L2 lateral horn); parasympathetic: craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4)
Sympathetic ganglia: paravertebral chain and prevertebral, close to cord (short pre-, long postganglionic); parasympathetic ganglia near or in target organs (long pre-, short post-)
All preganglionic neurons: ACh on nicotinic receptors; adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion
Postganglionic: parasympathetic ACh on muscarinic; sympathetic noradrenaline on α/β adrenoceptors
Exception: sympathetic cholinergic fibres to sweat glands (muscarinic)
questions.modelAnswer: The sympathetic division arises from preganglionic neurons in the lateral horn of the thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord (classically T1 to L2), so it is called thoracolumbar. Its ganglia lie close to the cord, in the paravertebral sympathetic chain or in prevertebral ganglia such as the coeliac and mesenteric ganglia, so preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres long. The parasympathetic division is craniosacral: preganglionic neurons lie in brainstem nuclei whose fibres run in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, and in the sacral cord (S2 to S4). Its ganglia lie in or near the organs they supply, so preganglionic fibres are long and postganglionic fibres short. In both divisions preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors on the postganglionic neuron. The adrenal medulla behaves as a modified sympathetic ganglion, receiving preganglionic fibres directly and releasing adrenaline into the blood. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors, whereas most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline onto α and β adrenoceptors. The important exception is the sympathetic supply to sweat glands, which is cholinergic and acts on muscarinic receptors.
questions.concept: Comparative anatomy and pharmacology of the autonomic divisions.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man had surgery that removed the hippocampus and nearby medial temporal structures on both sides. Which ability is most likely to be preserved?
options: Learning the names of new staff
Improving at a mirror-drawing task over several days
Recalling what he ate at his last meal
Learning the route to a new house
Remembering a conversation from an hour ago
questions.why: Bilateral medial temporal damage abolishes the formation of new declarative memories, but procedural learning depends on other systems (such as the striatum and cerebellum), so skills like mirror drawing still improve, as in patient H.M.
optWhy: Learning new names is new semantic (declarative) learning, which is impaired.
Correct: procedural skill learning is preserved, even without memory of practice.
Recalling a recent meal is new episodic memory.
Learning a new route depends on hippocampal spatial memory.
Recalling a recent conversation is new episodic (declarative) memory, which is lost.
questions.clue: "Removed the hippocampus... on both sides" and a list of new learning tasks.
questions.concept: Declarative versus non-declarative memory systems.

followUp.q: A 52-year-old with long-standing alcohol misuse cannot recall events from the past few hours and gives detailed but false accounts of his morning. Which structures are most likely damaged?
followUp.why: Korsakoff syndrome, from thiamine deficiency, damages the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus, causing severe amnesia with confabulation. Cerebellar vermis damage from alcohol causes gait ataxia, not amnesia; visual cortex and Broca's area damage cause visual and language deficits.

questions.q: A 67-year-old speaks fluently but with frequent paraphasias and made-up words, cannot follow simple commands and seems unaware that anything is wrong. Repetition is also poor. Which area is most likely damaged?
questions.why: Fluent paraphasic speech with poor comprehension, impaired repetition and poor insight is Wernicke's aphasia, from damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere.
optWhy: Right parietal damage causes neglect, not aphasia, in most people.
Left precentral gyrus damage causes right-sided weakness, possibly dysarthria, but not this aphasia.
Callosal section causes disconnection signs, not a fluent aphasia with poor comprehension.
The left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area) causes non-fluent speech with relatively good comprehension.
Correct: Wernicke's area in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus.
questions.clue: Fluent speech with neologisms, poor comprehension and no insight.
questions.concept: Classifying aphasia by fluency, comprehension and repetition.

followUp.q: After a stroke, a patient speaks fluently and understands well but cannot repeat "no ifs, ands or buts". Which aphasia is this?
followUp.why: Fluent speech and good comprehension with disproportionately impaired repetition define conduction aphasia. Broca's is non-fluent; Wernicke's has poor comprehension; transcortical aphasias preserve repetition.

questions.q: In most people, which hemisphere is dominant for language?
options: Right in right-handers and left in left-handers
Left in most right-handers and in most left-handers
questions.why: Most right-handed people and most left-handed people are left-hemisphere dominant for language; right or mixed dominance is more common among left-handers but still a minority.
optWhy: Language lateralisation does not depend on sex in this way.
Handedness does not simply flip language dominance; most left-handers are still left-dominant.
Correct: left dominance in most right-handers and most left-handers.
Right dominance is uncommon.
Language is strongly lateralised in most people.
questions.clue: "In most people".
questions.concept: Hemispheric dominance for language.

followUp.q: In a split-brain patient, a word is flashed only to the left visual field. What happens?
options: The patient cannot say the word but can pick the matching object with the left hand
The patient cannot see anything at all
The patient can say it but not point to it
The patient reads it aloud normally
followUp.why: The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere. Without the corpus callosum, the left (speaking) hemisphere does not receive it, so the word cannot be named, but the right hemisphere can guide the left hand to the matching object.

questions.q: A 45-year-old company director is brought by his wife. Over two years he has become rude and tactless, made inappropriate comments, overeaten sweet foods and spent money impulsively, and seems unconcerned. He can still find his way around and remembers recent events reasonably well. Which region is most affected?
questions.why: Disinhibition, socially inappropriate behaviour, impulsivity, dietary change and loss of insight with relatively preserved memory and navigation point to orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal (with anterior temporal) damage, as in behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia.
optWhy: Correct: orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal damage causes disinhibition and loss of social judgement.
Occipital damage causes visual deficits.
Right parietal damage causes neglect and spatial problems, and navigation is preserved here.
Cerebellar damage causes ataxia, not personality change.
Hippocampal damage causes early episodic memory loss, which is relatively mild here.
questions.clue: Rude, disinhibited, impulsive and unconcerned, with memory and navigation preserved.
questions.concept: Frontal lobe syndromes.

followUp.q: After a frontal head injury, a 35-year-old is polite and calm but cannot plan a shopping trip, perseverates on a sorting task when the rule changes and shows little initiative. Which region is most likely damaged?
followUp.why: Poor planning, perseveration on rule change (impaired set-shifting) and apathy indicate dysexecutive dysfunction from dorsolateral prefrontal damage. Orbitofrontal damage mainly causes disinhibition; motor cortex damage causes weakness; occipital damage affects vision.

questions.q: Distinguish declarative from non-declarative memory and give the brain structures most associated with each, using a classic case to illustrate.
markScheme: Declarative (explicit): episodic and semantic, consciously recalled
Depends on the medial temporal lobe (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex) for forming new memories; diencephalon (mammillary bodies, thalamus) also involved
Non-declarative (implicit): procedural skills/habits (striatum), conditioning (cerebellum; amygdala for emotional), priming (neocortex)
H.M.: bilateral MTL removal → severe anterograde amnesia but preserved mirror-drawing learning
Conclusion: separate memory systems; working memory (prefrontal) distinct again
questions.modelAnswer: Declarative or explicit memory is memory we can consciously report. It includes episodic memory for personal events and semantic memory for facts. Forming new declarative memories depends on the medial temporal lobe, especially the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, together with diencephalic structures such as the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus. Non-declarative or implicit memory is expressed through performance rather than recollection. It includes procedural skills and habits, which depend on the striatum; classical conditioning, which depends on the cerebellum for motor responses and the amygdala for emotional responses; and priming. The case of H.M. illustrates the distinction. After bilateral removal of his medial temporal lobes to control severe seizures he could not form new declarative memories, so he could not remember people he had just met. Yet his performance on a mirror-drawing task improved across days even though he had no memory of practising it. This shows that procedural learning uses systems outside the hippocampus.
questions.concept: Multiple memory systems and their anatomy.

questions.q: A drug increases how often GABA-A chloride channels open, but only when GABA is present. Which drug class is this?
questions.why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators at the α/γ interface of GABA-A receptors; they increase opening frequency in the presence of GABA but do not open the channel on their own.
optWhy: NMDA antagonists block glutamate receptor channels.
Opioid agonists act on G-protein-coupled opioid receptors.
Barbiturates mainly prolong channel opening and can open it directly at high concentrations.
Correct: benzodiazepines increase opening frequency and need GABA.
GABA-B agonists such as baclofen act on G-protein-coupled receptors, not the Cl⁻ channel.
questions.clue: "Increases how often... only when GABA is present".
questions.concept: Benzodiazepine mechanism at GABA-A receptors.

followUp.q: Why is an overdose of a benzodiazepine alone usually less dangerous than an overdose of a barbiturate?
options: Benzodiazepines act only in the spinal cord
Benzodiazepines do not cross the blood–brain barrier
Benzodiazepines need GABA to act and do not open the channel directly
followUp.why: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA's own effect, so their action has a ceiling, whereas barbiturates can open the channel directly at high concentrations. The risk rises sharply when benzodiazepines are combined with alcohol or opioids. They do cross the blood–brain barrier and are not antagonists.

questions.q: A 24-year-old starting a typical antipsychotic for schizophrenia has fewer hallucinations, but develops stiffness, a tremor and galactorrhoea. Blockade of D2 receptors in which pathways best explains, in order, the benefit, the stiffness and the galactorrhoea?
questions.why: Positive psychotic symptoms are linked to mesolimbic dopamine overactivity, so D2 blockade there helps. Blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway causes parkinsonism. Dopamine from the tuberoinfundibular pathway inhibits prolactin release, so blockade raises prolactin and can cause galactorrhoea.
optWhy: Mesocortical blockade is not the source of benefit for hallucinations and may worsen negative symptoms.
Correct: mesolimbic (benefit), nigrostriatal (stiffness), tuberoinfundibular (galactorrhoea).
Nigrostriatal blockade causes stiffness, not the antipsychotic benefit.
Tuberoinfundibular blockade raises prolactin; it does not relieve hallucinations.
This swaps the pathways for stiffness and galactorrhoea.
questions.clue: Fewer hallucinations, then stiffness and tremor, then galactorrhoea.
questions.concept: Dopamine pathways and antipsychotic effects.

followUp.q: A woman taking an antipsychotic has amenorrhoea and a raised serum prolactin. Which explanation is correct?
options: The drug stimulates prolactin-secreting cells directly
D2 blockade removes tuberoinfundibular dopamine's inhibition of prolactin release
followUp.why: Dopamine from the tuberoinfundibular pathway tonically inhibits prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary; D2 blockade releases this brake. The nigrostriatal pathway concerns movement, and the antipsychotic does not stimulate lactotrophs directly.

questions.q: A 26-year-old taking an SSRI is given tramadol after dental surgery. The next day she is agitated and sweaty, with a temperature of 38.6 °C, heart rate 124/min, dilated pupils, diarrhoea, brisk reflexes and inducible ankle clonus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Two serotonergic drugs, rapid onset, autonomic instability and neuromuscular hyperactivity with inducible clonus fit serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria). Management centres on stopping the serotonergic drugs and supportive care.
optWhy: Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin and normal reflexes, not sweating and clonus.
Opioid toxicity causes pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and slow breathing.
Malignant hyperthermia follows volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium.
NMS follows dopamine blockade, evolves over days and causes lead-pipe rigidity with reduced reflexes.
Correct: SSRI plus tramadol with clonus and hyperreflexia.
questions.clue: SSRI plus tramadol; sweating, hyperthermia, brisk reflexes and inducible clonus.
questions.concept: Recognising serotonin syndrome.

followUp.q: A 40-year-old started on a high-potency antipsychotic five days ago has a temperature of 39.5 °C, severe generalised rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, labile blood pressure and a very high creatine kinase. Reflexes are reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
followUp.why: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability and very high CK developing over days after dopamine blockade indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Serotonin syndrome is faster with clonus and hyperreflexia; acute dystonia causes sustained muscle spasms without fever.

questions.q: A 35-year-old is brought in after an overdose of amitriptyline. He is drowsy with dilated pupils, a heart rate of 125/min and a blood pressure of 88/50 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 0.14 s. Which drug action explains the QRS widening?
options: Fast sodium channel blockade in the conducting system and myocardium
questions.why: Tricyclic antidepressants block fast Na⁺ channels in the His–Purkinje system and myocardium, slowing depolarisation and widening the QRS; a broad QRS predicts arrhythmias and seizures. Antimuscarinic effects cause the tachycardia and dilated pupils, and α₁ blockade contributes to hypotension.
optWhy: H1 blockade causes sedation, not conduction delay.
Muscarinic blockade explains tachycardia and dilated pupils, not QRS widening.
Correct: Na⁺ channel blockade widens the QRS.
α₁ blockade causes vasodilation and hypotension, not QRS widening.
Reuptake inhibition is the therapeutic action and does not widen the QRS.
questions.clue: Amitriptyline overdose with QRS 0.14 s.
questions.concept: Mechanisms of tricyclic toxicity.

followUp.q: A patient with an opioid overdose has a GCS of 8, a respiratory rate of 6/min and pinpoint pupils. Which drug action is the basis for reversing this?
followUp.why: Naloxone competitively displaces opioids from μ receptors, reversing respiratory depression and sedation; it may need repeating because its action can be shorter than that of the opioid. The other mechanisms do not reverse opioid effects (no doses are given here).

questions.q: Explain why typical antipsychotics may relieve hallucinations but cause parkinsonism and galactorrhoea.
markScheme: Typical antipsychotics are D2 receptor antagonists
Mesolimbic dopamine overactivity linked to positive symptoms; blockade relieves hallucinations and delusions
Nigrostriatal blockade → reduced D2 signalling in the striatum (indirect pathway disinhibited) → parkinsonism and other extrapyramidal effects
Tuberoinfundibular dopamine inhibits prolactin release; blockade → hyperprolactinaemia → galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction
Drug acts on all pathways at once; atypical drugs (5-HT2A blockade, lower D2 affinity) tend to cause fewer extrapyramidal effects
questions.modelAnswer: Typical antipsychotics work mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors, and the drug reaches all dopamine pathways at once. Positive psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions are linked to overactivity of the mesolimbic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, so blocking D2 receptors there relieves them. The same blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway, from the substantia nigra to the striatum, reproduces the dopamine deficiency of Parkinson's disease: the indirect pathway is released, output-nucleus inhibition of the thalamus rises, and the patient develops bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor, as well as other extrapyramidal effects such as acute dystonia and akathisia. In the tuberoinfundibular pathway, dopamine released into the pituitary portal circulation normally inhibits prolactin secretion. Blocking D2 receptors on lactotrophs removes this brake, raising prolactin and causing galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and sexual dysfunction. Atypical antipsychotics, which also block 5-HT2A receptors or bind D2 receptors less tightly, tend to cause fewer extrapyramidal effects, though they have their own adverse effects.
questions.concept: Pathway-specific effects of D2 blockade.

questions.q: Which is the most characteristic CSF finding in Guillain–Barré syndrome?
options: Raised protein with a normal cell count
Raised neutrophil count with low glucose
questions.why: Albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein with a normal white cell count) is characteristic, though protein may be normal in the first days.
optWhy: Correct: high protein with a normal cell count.
Xanthochromia indicates subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Lymphocytosis suggests viral meningitis or other inflammation, not typical GBS.
CSF may be normal early, but the characteristic finding is raised protein without cells.
Neutrophils with low glucose suggest bacterial meningitis.
questions.clue: "Most characteristic CSF finding".
questions.concept: CSF patterns in neurological disease.

followUp.q: A 20-year-old has fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. CSF shows 1,500 white cells ×10⁶/L (mostly neutrophils), protein 2.4 g/L and a CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.2. Which is most likely?
followUp.why: Neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein and a glucose ratio below 0.5 indicate bacterial meningitis. Viral meningitis has lymphocytes and a normal glucose ratio; GBS has high protein without cells; SAH shows red cells and xanthochromia.

questions.q: A 67-year-old has a 6-month history of a slow right hand, a right hand tremor at rest and reduced right arm swing. Examination confirms asymmetric bradykinesia with rigidity. According to NICE NG71, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Request a DaT (FP-CIT SPECT) scan in all cases
Start levodopa and review in 3 months
Request an MRI brain to confirm the diagnosis
Refer quickly and untreated to a specialist in Parkinson's disease
questions.why: NICE NG71 advises referring people with suspected Parkinson's disease quickly and untreated to a specialist, who makes a clinical diagnosis using the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria.
optWhy: FP-CIT SPECT is considered only when essential tremor cannot be distinguished clinically from parkinsonism.
Starting treatment before specialist assessment can obscure the diagnosis; NG71 says refer untreated.
NG71 says not to use structural MRI to diagnose Parkinson's disease.
Correct: quick, untreated referral to a specialist.
NG71 advises against objective smell testing in the differential diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes outside trials.
questions.clue: "According to NICE NG71" and suspected Parkinson's disease in primary care.
questions.concept: Diagnostic pathway for suspected Parkinson's disease.

followUp.q: A 60-year-old has a symmetrical action tremor of both hands. The specialist cannot clinically distinguish essential tremor from parkinsonism. Which test does NICE NG71 suggest considering?
followUp.why: NG71 suggests considering 123I-FP-CIT SPECT when essential tremor cannot be clinically differentiated from parkinsonism, because it shows reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter uptake in degenerative parkinsonism. Structural MRI is not used to diagnose PD; LP and EEG do not help here.

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman had painful loss of vision in one eye that recovered over weeks. A year later she develops numbness of both legs, which worsens briefly after a hot bath. Which investigation best supports the likely diagnosis?
options: MRI of the brain and spinal cord
questions.why: Optic neuritis followed by a spinal cord syndrome, separated in time, with heat sensitivity, suggests multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain and spinal cord shows lesions disseminated in space and time, the core of the McDonald criteria.
optWhy: Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves, which are not the problem in MS.
Correct: MRI shows characteristic demyelinating lesions.
AChR antibodies are used for myasthenia gravis.
Muscle biopsy is for myopathies.
CT is far less sensitive than MRI for demyelinating lesions.
questions.clue: Optic neuritis, then leg numbness a year later, worse with heat.
questions.concept: Diagnosing MS: dissemination in space and time on MRI.

followUp.q: A 33-year-old has a single episode of painful visual loss in the right eye with a right relative afferent pupillary defect. MRI shows several periventricular and juxtacortical lesions. Under the 2024 McDonald revision, which site has been added as a fifth location for dissemination in space?
followUp.why: The 2024 McDonald revisions (published in 2025) added the optic nerve as a fifth CNS region for dissemination in space, alongside periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord regions. Peripheral nerves and the pituitary are not CNS demyelination sites in the criteria, and the cerebellum is part of the infratentorial region already.

questions.q: A 48-year-old has a sudden, severe "worst ever" headache that peaked within a minute while lifting. She is alert with no focal signs. A non-contrast CT head performed 3 hours after onset is normal. According to NICE NG228, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with simple analgesia without further thought
Perform a lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset
Do not routinely offer a lumbar puncture; consider other diagnoses
questions.why: NG228 notes that CT is most accurate within 6 hours of onset; if a CT done within 6 hours is negative, lumbar puncture is not routinely offered and other diagnoses should be considered (senior review remains appropriate). Lumbar puncture, at least 12 hours after onset, is considered when a CT done more than 6 hours after onset is negative.
optWhy: A thunderclap headache still needs assessment for other serious causes, so discharge without thought is unsafe.
A thunderclap headache should not be assumed to be migraine.
An immediate LP is too early to detect bilirubin and is not routinely indicated after an early negative CT.
This is the approach for a negative CT performed more than 6 hours after onset, not within 6 hours.
Correct: an early negative CT means LP is not routinely offered; consider other causes.
questions.clue: Thunderclap headache with a normal CT "3 hours after onset".
questions.concept: NICE NG228 diagnostic pathway for suspected SAH.

followUp.q: A 52-year-old with a thunderclap headache has a normal CT head performed 9 hours after onset. What does NICE NG228 recommend considering?
options: Immediate lumbar puncture regardless of time
Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after symptom onset
followUp.why: If CT is negative but was performed more than 6 hours after onset, NG228 recommends considering lumbar puncture, waiting until at least 12 hours after onset so bilirubin (xanthochromia) can be detected. An EEG has no role here.

questions.q: A 74-year-old had sudden weakness of the left arm and face with slurred speech while making breakfast. It lasted 40 minutes and resolved fully before arrival. Examination is now normal and CT is not yet done. According to NICE NG128, what is the most appropriate management?
options: Arrange outpatient MRI and see the GP in 2 weeks
Calculate an ABCD2 score to decide the urgency of referral
Give aspirin immediately (unless contraindicated) and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours
Reassure and refer routinely to the neurology clinic
questions.why: Transient focal symptoms with full recovery suggest a TIA. NG128 advises aspirin immediately unless contraindicated and specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset, and says not to use scores such as ABCD2 to decide urgency.
optWhy: Delaying assessment for two weeks is unsafe.
NG128 recommends against using ABCD2 or similar scores to assess risk or decide urgency.
Correct: immediate aspirin and specialist assessment within 24 hours.
Thrombolysis is for a persisting deficit from ischaemic stroke, not resolved symptoms.
Routine referral is too slow: early stroke risk after TIA is high.
questions.clue: Transient symptoms for 40 minutes, now resolved; "according to NICE NG128".
questions.concept: Initial management of suspected TIA.

followUp.q: A 66-year-old has had left face, arm and leg weakness and dysarthria for 90 minutes. CT head shows no haemorrhage. There are no contraindications. According to NICE NG128, which treatment should be offered?
options: Thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase), with thrombectomy if a proximal large-vessel occlusion is confirmed
Wait for MRI before any treatment
followUp.why: Within 4.5 hours, with haemorrhage excluded and no contraindications, thrombolysis is offered; thrombectomy is added for confirmed proximal anterior circulation occlusion within 6 hours. Waiting for MRI delays treatment; aspirin alone misses the window; immediate anticoagulation is not the treatment for acute ischaemic stroke.

questions.q: Outline the initial hospital management of a patient arriving 2 hours after the onset of a suspected acute ischaemic stroke, according to NICE guidance (no doses).
markScheme: Rapid assessment (ABCDE), recognise stroke, check capillary glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
Immediate non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage; CT angiography if thrombectomy may be indicated
Thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) within 4.5 hours if no contraindications
Thrombectomy for confirmed proximal anterior circulation occlusion within 6 hours (with thrombolysis if eligible)
Aspirin as soon as possible and within 24 hours once haemorrhage excluded; glucose kept 4–11 mmol/L; swallow screen; admission to a stroke unit
questions.modelAnswer: The patient should be assessed rapidly using an ABCDE approach, with the stroke team alerted and a capillary blood glucose checked, because hypoglycaemia can mimic a stroke. Because he is within the treatment window, he needs immediate non-contrast CT of the head to exclude haemorrhage, with CT angiography if thrombectomy might be appropriate. Under NICE NG128, if CT excludes haemorrhage and there are no contraindications, thrombolysis with tenecteplase or alteplase should be given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. If CT angiography confirms a proximal large-vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation, thrombectomy should be offered as soon as possible within 6 hours, together with thrombolysis if he is eligible. Aspirin is started as soon as possible and within 24 hours once haemorrhage has been excluded. Blood glucose should be kept between 4 and 11 mmol/L, swallowing assessed before oral intake, and he should be admitted directly to an acute stroke unit. Doses are not given here.
questions.concept: Time-critical management of acute ischaemic stroke.

questions.q: "Long-term potentiation is the cellular basis of learning and memory." Critically evaluate this statement with reference to the mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and the experimental evidence linking it to behaviour.
markScheme: Defines LTP (a lasting increase in synaptic strength after high-frequency or paired activity) and its discovery by Bliss and Lømo (1973) in the hippocampus
Explains induction: glutamate plus postsynaptic depolarisation relieves the NMDA receptor Mg²⁺ block; Ca²⁺ entry activates kinases
Explains expression: more or more effective AMPA receptors (and possibly presynaptic changes; the balance is debated)
Notes properties that fit a memory mechanism: input specificity, associativity, persistence (Hebbian)
Cites behavioural evidence: NMDA antagonist AP5 impairs spatial water-maze learning (Morris et al., 1986) at doses that block LTP
Gives limitations: blocking LTP does not abolish all learning; correlation is not proof; definitive proof in behaving animals is lacking
Considers other forms of plasticity (LTD, homeostatic plasticity) and non-hippocampal memory systems (striatum, cerebellum)
Reaches a balanced conclusion: LTP-like plasticity is a strong candidate mechanism for some forms of memory, not the sole basis
questions.modelAnswer:
Long-term potentiation is a persistent increase in the strength of synaptic transmission following brief high-frequency or paired activity. Bliss and Lømo described it in 1973 in the dentate gyrus of anaesthetised rabbits after stimulation of the perforant path. Because the hippocampus had already been linked to declarative memory by the case of H.M., LTP quickly became the leading candidate for a cellular memory mechanism.

The mechanism at the classic CA1 and dentate synapses depends on NMDA receptors. At rest these channels are blocked by Mg²⁺; when strong input depolarises the postsynaptic membrane through AMPA receptors while glutamate is bound, the block is expelled and Ca²⁺ enters the spine. Ca²⁺ activates kinases such as CaMKII, leading to more AMPA receptors in the synapse, greater single-channel conductance and possibly increased transmitter release; the relative contribution of pre- and postsynaptic change is still debated. Later phases need gene transcription and protein synthesis.

Several properties make LTP an attractive memory mechanism. It is input-specific (only active synapses strengthen), associative (a weak input paired with a strong one is potentiated) and can persist for long periods. These are the properties Hebb proposed for learning.

Behavioural evidence supports a link. Morris and colleagues (1986) showed that infusing the NMDA antagonist AP5 impaired learning in a water maze at doses that blocked hippocampal LTP, while a visual discrimination task was spared. Genetic manipulations of NMDA receptor subunits and kinases have given broadly similar results.

However, the statement overreaches. Blocking LTP does not abolish all learning, and animals can sometimes learn spatial tasks under NMDA blockade if pretrained. Correlation between LTP and learning is not proof of causation, and reviewers note that definitive proof that LTP mechanisms underlie memory in the behaving animal is still lacking. Other forms of plasticity, such as long-term depression and homeostatic scaling, are also needed. And many forms of memory, such as procedural skills (striatum) and eyeblink conditioning (cerebellum), depend on different circuits with their own plasticity rules.

In conclusion, LTP and related synaptic plasticity are the best-supported cellular candidates for at least hippocampus-dependent memory, but "the" cellular basis of all learning and memory is too strong a claim.
questions.concept: Synaptic plasticity and the evidence linking LTP to memory.

questions.q: Mr Colin Barker, 64, has noticed weakness of his right hand for six months, with difficulty turning keys. More recently his walking has become clumsy and his speech slurred. Examination shows wasting of the small muscles of both hands, fasciculation in the forearms and thighs, brisk biceps and knee reflexes and extensor plantars. Sensation is normal. (a) Classify each sign as UMN or LMN and explain its mechanism. (b) What is the most likely diagnosis and the key differential? (c) Outline the principles of investigation and management.
markScheme: Wasting: LMN, loss of trophic innervation of muscle fibres
Fasciculation: LMN, spontaneous discharges of diseased motor units
Brisk reflexes and extensor plantars: UMN, loss of descending control of intact spinal reflex arcs
Combination of UMN and LMN signs in several regions with normal sensation → motor neurone disease
Key differential: cervical myelopathy with radiculopathy (neck pain, sensory signs, sphincter involvement); also multifocal motor neuropathy, myasthenia
Investigations: neurophysiology (EMG/nerve conduction), MRI of cervical spine (exclude structural cause), bloods; specialist neurology assessment

Management: multidisciplinary team, speech and swallowing, nutrition, breathing assessment with non-invasive ventilation where appropriate (NICE NG42), disease-modifying drug discussed by specialist, advance care planning
Communication: honest discussion of prognosis, involving the patient in decisions
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Wasting of the small hand muscles is a lower motor neuron sign: when the anterior horn cell or its axon degenerates, the muscle fibres lose their innervation and atrophy. Fasciculation is also an LMN sign; it reflects spontaneous discharge of a diseased motor unit, visible as a flicker under the skin. Brisk biceps and knee reflexes and extensor plantar responses are upper motor neuron signs: the reflex arcs are intact, but loss of descending corticospinal and related control removes inhibition, so stretch reflexes are exaggerated and the primitive extensor plantar response returns. Slurred speech may reflect bulbar involvement of either type.

(b) Finding UMN and LMN signs together in the same regions, affecting several body regions, with normal sensation, strongly suggests motor neurone disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis type). The most important differential is cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy, which can give LMN signs in the arms and UMN signs in the legs; neck pain, sensory signs and sphincter disturbance favour it. Bulbar involvement and fasciculation in the legs would not be explained by a cervical lesion. Other considerations include multifocal motor neuropathy (pure LMN) and, for bulbar symptoms, myasthenia gravis.

(c) He needs prompt specialist neurology assessment. Neurophysiology (EMG and nerve conduction studies) looks for widespread denervation with normal sensory responses. MRI of the cervical spine and brain excludes a structural cause, and blood tests exclude mimics. Management is multidisciplinary and supportive: information and psychological support, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, dietetic assessment of swallowing and nutrition (including gastrostomy when appropriate), and regular assessment of respiratory function, with non-invasive ventilation offered when indicated, as NICE NG42 sets out. A specialist will discuss disease-modifying treatment. Early advance care planning respects his wishes as the disease progresses. Doses are not given here.
questions.concept: Integrating UMN and LMN signs to diagnose and manage MND.

questions.q: Mr Edward Lam, 71, a right-handed retired teacher, is admitted after a stroke. His speech is slow, halting and effortful, mainly nouns ("Wife… car… hospital"). He follows simple commands but struggles with complex grammatical instructions, cannot repeat phrases and is clearly frustrated. He also has weakness of the right face and arm. (a) Classify his language disorder and localise the lesion, explaining your reasoning. (b) How would you distinguish it from Wernicke's and conduction aphasia, and from dysarthria? (c) Which vascular territory is involved, and what other features might you look for? (d) How does his deficit affect communication and consent, and how would you support him?
markScheme: Broca's (non-fluent, expressive) aphasia: effortful, telegraphic speech, relatively preserved comprehension, impaired repetition, insight preserved
Lesion: left posterior inferior frontal gyrus (dominant), close to face/arm motor cortex, explaining right face/arm weakness
Wernicke's: fluent, paraphasic, poor comprehension, poor insight; conduction: fluent, good comprehension, repetition disproportionately impaired
Dysarthria: abnormal articulation with intact language (normal writing, comprehension, grammar)
Territory: left MCA (superior division); look for hemianopia, sensory loss, apraxia; Oxford classification (PACS if no hemianopia)
Bedside testing: spontaneous speech, comprehension of graded commands, repetition, naming, reading, writing
Capacity is decision-specific; aphasia does not equal lack of capacity; use simple language, yes/no questions, pictures, writing, time
Speech and language therapy, involve family, document communication methods
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Mr Lam has Broca's (non-fluent, expressive) aphasia. His speech is slow, effortful and telegraphic, made up mostly of content words without grammatical words. Comprehension of simple commands is preserved, though complex grammar is hard, and repetition is impaired. He is aware of his difficulty and frustrated, which is typical. Broca's aphasia arises from damage to the posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere; he is right-handed, so this is very likely the left hemisphere. The adjacent face and arm area of the motor cortex explains his right face and arm weakness.

(b) In Wernicke's aphasia speech is fluent with normal rhythm but contains paraphasias and neologisms, comprehension is poor and insight is often lacking. In conduction aphasia speech is fluent and comprehension good, but repetition is disproportionately poor. Dysarthria is a disorder of articulation from weakness or incoordination of the speech muscles: speech sounds slurred, but word choice, grammar, comprehension, reading and writing are normal. Asking the patient to write is a quick way to separate them.

(c) The lesion lies in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery, typically its superior division, which supplies the inferior frontal and adjacent motor cortex. Other features to check include a right homonymous hemianopia, sensory loss, apraxia and swallowing difficulty. Under the Oxford classification, weakness of face and arm plus higher cortical dysfunction without hemianopia is a partial anterior circulation syndrome.

(d) Aphasia makes communication hard but does not by itself mean he lacks capacity, which is decision-specific. Clinicians should use short sentences, closed questions, gesture, pictures, written key words and extra time, check understanding, and involve a speech and language therapist, who can also advise on communication aids. Family members can help but should not decide for him if he has capacity. Methods that work should be documented so the whole team uses them.
questions.concept: Classifying and localising aphasia and supporting communication.

questions.q: Mr Daniel Kerr, 52, has had Parkinson's disease for 9 years. His motor symptoms were initially well controlled with levodopa (with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor), but he now has "wearing off" before each dose, sudden "off" periods and writhing involuntary movements at peak dose. A dopamine agonist was added a year ago, and his wife reports he has started gambling online. (a) Explain why levodopa is combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor. (b) Explain the mechanisms of wearing off and peak-dose dyskinesia. (c) What are the pharmacological strategies used to smooth the response (no doses)? (d) Explain the new behaviour and how it should be managed, with reference to NICE guidance.
markScheme: Levodopa crosses the BBB via amino-acid transport and is decarboxylated to dopamine; peripheral decarboxylation causes nausea and wastes drug; inhibitor (does not cross BBB) increases central delivery
Wearing off: loss of presynaptic nigral terminals reduces storage/buffering, so striatal dopamine tracks plasma levodopa with a short half-life
Peak-dose dyskinesia: pulsatile stimulation of sensitised postsynaptic receptors produces involuntary movements at high levels

Strategies: more frequent smaller doses or modified-release levodopa, adding COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, dopamine agonists, amantadine for dyskinesia, advanced therapies (deep brain stimulation, infusions) via specialist
Gambling = impulse control disorder associated with dopamine agonists (NICE NG71); risk factors include agonist therapy, history of impulsive behaviour, alcohol/smoking
Management: discuss sensitively with patient and family, review and gradually reduce agonist under specialist guidance (beware dopamine agonist withdrawal), practical safeguards
NICE NG71: inform patients starting agonists of ICD risk and monitor; record discussion
Overall: multidisciplinary specialist management; no doses
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Dopamine itself does not cross the blood–brain barrier, but its precursor levodopa does, via an amino-acid transporter, and is converted to dopamine in the brain by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase. Given alone, much of the levodopa would be decarboxylated in the gut wall and blood, wasting the drug and producing peripheral dopamine that causes nausea and hypotension. A peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor such as carbidopa or benserazide does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it blocks this conversion outside the brain only, increasing the amount of levodopa reaching the brain and reducing peripheral adverse effects.

(b) Early in the disease, surviving nigral terminals take up dopamine made from levodopa, store it and release it steadily, so each dose lasts many hours. As more terminals are lost this buffer disappears, and striatal dopamine starts to follow the plasma levodopa level, which falls quickly. Symptoms then return before the next dose (wearing off), and erratic gut absorption can cause sudden "off" periods. Pulsatile stimulation also sensitises postsynaptic striatal receptors, so at peak plasma levels excessive stimulation produces writhing choreiform movements (peak-dose dyskinesia).

(c) The aim is more continuous dopaminergic stimulation.
