Options include dividing levodopa into smaller, more frequent doses or using modified-release preparations, adding a COMT inhibitor or MAO-B inhibitor to slow dopamine breakdown, and dopamine agonists, which have a longer action. Amantadine can reduce dyskinesia. For selected patients, specialists may consider deep brain stimulation or continuous drug infusions. These decisions belong to the specialist team, and no doses are given here.

(d) New gambling is very likely an impulse control disorder. NICE NG71 notes that dopamine agonist therapy, a history of impulsive behaviour, and alcohol consumption or smoking increase the risk. Patients starting agonists should be told about this risk, and it should be monitored. He and his wife need a sensitive, non-judgemental discussion, and the specialist team should review his treatment, usually reducing the dopamine agonist gradually because sudden withdrawal can cause a withdrawal syndrome. Practical safeguards such as financial controls may help, and the discussion and plan should be documented.
questions.concept: Levodopa pharmacology, motor complications and impulse control disorders.

cases.title: Sudden weakness at breakfast

steps.text: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Her husband says that at 07:30, while eating breakfast, she suddenly dropped her cup and her speech became garbled. It is now 08:45. She has atrial fibrillation and takes no anticoagulant.

ask.q: What is the first bedside test to do after the ABCDE assessment?
ask.why: Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke and is quickly reversible, so capillary glucose is checked straight away. Lumbar puncture and EEG are not first-line tests for suspected stroke, and ESR does not change immediate management.

steps.text: Glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. She has right face and arm weakness more than leg, a right homonymous hemianopia and expressive dysphasia. BP is 168/94 mmHg and the rhythm is atrial fibrillation.

ask.q: Which arterial territory and Oxford classification fit best?
options: Right MCA, partial anterior circulation syndrome
Left MCA, total anterior circulation syndrome
ask.why: Right face and arm weakness, right homonymous hemianopia and dysphasia (higher cortical dysfunction) are all present: a total anterior circulation syndrome in the left MCA territory. The right MCA would cause left-sided signs; the ACA spares the face and arm relatively; posterior circulation strokes cause brainstem or cerebellar signs or isolated hemianopia.

steps.text: Non-contrast CT at 09:05 shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows occlusion of the proximal left middle cerebral artery. She has no contraindications to thrombolysis.

ask.q: According to NICE NG128, what should be offered?
options: Wait for MRI to confirm infarction
Thrombolysis and thrombectomy as soon as possible
Aspirin only and admit to the ward
ask.why: She is within 4.5 hours of onset for thrombolysis and within 6 hours for thrombectomy of a proximal anterior circulation occlusion, so both should be offered as soon as possible. Aspirin alone would miss reperfusion; immediate anticoagulation is not used in acute ischaemic stroke; waiting for MRI wastes salvageable tissue.

steps.text: Outcome: after reperfusion her arm strength improves over the next day. She is admitted to the stroke unit, has a swallow screen before eating, and the team plans secondary prevention, including anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation at a time judged safe by the stroke team (no doses given here).

debrief: Check glucose early: hypoglycaemia mimics stroke.
Localise the stroke from the pattern of deficits and classify it (Oxford/Bamford).
Non-contrast CT excludes haemorrhage; CT angiography identifies large-vessel occlusion.
NICE NG128: thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and thrombectomy for proximal anterior occlusion within 6 hours (up to 24 hours if salvageable brain).
Atrial fibrillation is a major cause of cardioembolic stroke.

cases.title: The worst headache ever

steps.text: A 48-year-old woman developed a sudden, severe headache while lifting a heavy box; it reached maximum intensity within a minute. She vomited once. She has no previous similar headaches.

ask.q: Which feature makes this a red-flag headache?
options: Thunderclap onset (peak within about a minute)
ask.why: A thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within about a minute raises concern for subarachnoid haemorrhage. Vomiting is common in many headaches, including migraine, and age alone and time of day are not the key feature here.

steps.text: GCS is 15, with neck stiffness but no focal deficit. Temperature 37.1 °C. NEWS2 is 1. A non-contrast CT head performed 2 hours after onset shows blood in the basal cisterns.

ask.q: What is the next investigation recommended by NICE NG228?
ask.why: Once SAH is confirmed on CT, NG228 recommends CT angiography without delay to find the aneurysm. Lumbar puncture is used only when CT is negative; EEG has no role; delaying imaging risks rebleeding before the aneurysm is treated.

steps.text: CT angiography shows an anterior communicating artery aneurysm. The neurosurgical team is contacted.

ask.q: Which drug does NICE NG228 recommend considering after confirmed aneurysmal SAH (no doses)?
ask.why: NG228 recommends considering enteral nimodipine after confirmed SAH (intravenous use only in specialist settings). Thrombolytics and aspirin would increase bleeding risk; triptans are for migraine.

steps.text: Outcome: the aneurysm is secured by the specialist team. Over the following weeks she is monitored for complications such as rebleeding, delayed cerebral ischaemia and hydrocephalus (from impaired CSF absorption).

debrief: A thunderclap headache is a red flag for subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Non-contrast CT is most accurate within 6 hours of onset; if CT after 6 hours is negative, consider LP at least 12 hours after onset.
Confirmed SAH: CT angiography without delay, then specialist aneurysm treatment.
Hydrocephalus after SAH reflects impaired CSF absorption (communicating hydrocephalus).

osce.title: Upper limb neurological examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about pain; expose both arms
General inspection: posture, wasting, fasciculation, tremor, scars, walking aids or other clues around the bed
Pronator drift: arms outstretched with palms up, then eyes closed; look for pronation and downward drift (subtle UMN weakness)
Tone at shoulder, elbow and wrist on each side, noting spasticity, rigidity (including cogwheeling) or hypotonia
Power using the MRC scale, comparing sides: shoulder abduction (C5), elbow flexion (C5/6) and extension (C7), wrist extension (C6), finger extension (C7), finger abduction (T1), thumb abduction (T1)
Reflexes: biceps (C5/6), supinator (C5/6) and triceps (C7), using reinforcement if absent
Sensation: light touch and pinprick by dermatome with the eyes closed, comparing sides; then vibration and joint position sense starting distally
Coordination: finger–nose testing and rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia)
Thank the patient, clean your hands, summarise findings (UMN, LMN, sensory or cerebellar pattern) and suggest next steps (e.g. full neurological examination, imaging)
tips: Always compare left with right at each step.
Decide the pattern (UMN, LMN, sensory, cerebellar, extrapyramidal) before naming a cause.
Check power before interpreting coordination: weakness can mimic ataxia.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.

osce.title: Lower limb neurological examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain, gain consent and ask about pain; expose the legs while maintaining dignity
General inspection: wasting, fasciculation, scars, deformity (e.g. pes cavus), walking aids
Gait, including heel-to-toe walking, and Romberg's test (unsteadiness only with the eyes closed suggests a proprioceptive or vestibular problem); stand close for safety
Tone: roll the legs, lift the knee briskly, and test for ankle clonus
Power: hip flexion (L1/2), hip extension, knee extension (L3/4), knee flexion, ankle dorsiflexion (L4/5), plantarflexion (S1/2) and big toe extension (L5)
Reflexes: knee (L3/4), ankle (S1) and plantar response
Sensation by dermatome (light touch, pinprick), then vibration and joint position sense distally first
Coordination: heel–shin test
Thank the patient, clean your hands, summarise and suggest further assessment (e.g. upper limb and cranial nerve examination, imaging)
tips: A positive Romberg's test points to sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia, not cerebellar disease.
More than a few beats of ankle clonus is a UMN sign.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.

osce.title: Cranial nerve examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about pain; sit the patient facing you at eye level
General inspection: facial asymmetry, ptosis, pupil asymmetry, abnormal eye position, speech, and clues such as glasses or hearing aids
Olfactory (I): ask about any change in sense of smell
Optic (II): visual acuity with a Snellen chart (with glasses or pinhole), visual fields by confrontation, and offer colour vision and fundoscopy
Pupils (II and III): inspect size, then direct and consensual light reflexes, the swinging light test for a relative afferent pupillary defect, and accommodation
Eye movements (III, IV, VI): follow a target in an H pattern, asking about double vision and watching for nystagmus and ptosis
Trigeminal (V): facial sensation in V1, V2 and V3 on both sides; jaw muscle bulk and jaw opening against resistance; offer the corneal reflex
Facial (VII): raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly, puff out cheeks, smile; note whether the forehead is spared (UMN) or involved (LMN)
Vestibulocochlear (VIII): whispered voice test, then Rinne and Weber tests with a 512 Hz tuning fork
Glossopharyngeal and vagus (IX, X): voice, cough, palate elevation and uvula position; ask about swallowing
Accessory (XI): shoulder shrug and head turn against resistance
Hypoglossal (XII): tongue at rest for wasting and fasciculation, then on protrusion for deviation (towards the weak side)
Thank the patient, clean your hands, summarise findings and suggest further assessment (e.g. full neurological examination, imaging)
tips: An UMN facial weakness spares the forehead because the upper face receives input from both hemispheres.
In a relative afferent pupillary defect both pupils dilate when the light swings to the affected eye.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.

interpret.title: Peaked T waves on a lead II strip
interpret.q: A 72-year-old with acute kidney injury feels weak. Lead II at 25 mm/s shows a regular rhythm with a P wave before each QRS, R–R interval 21 small squares, PR 4 small squares, QRS 2.5 small squares and tall, narrow, peaked T waves. Which disturbance best fits, and why does it alter excitability?
options: First-degree heart block from vagal tone
Hypokalaemia: hyperpolarised cells are more excitable
Hyperkalaemia: a less negative resting potential leaves Na⁺ channels partly inactivated
Hypercalcaemia: Ca²⁺ blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels
Sinus tachycardia from anxiety: no electrolyte problem
interpret.why: R–R = 21 × 0.04 = 0.84 s, so the rate is about 71/min with normal PR (0.16 s) and QRS (0.10 s) in sinus rhythm. Peaked T waves are the classic early ECG sign of hyperkalaemia: raised extracellular K⁺ makes E_K and the resting potential less negative and speeds repolarisation, and sustained depolarisation inactivates Na⁺ channels, so conduction and excitability eventually fall.
optWhy: First-degree block needs a PR over 0.20 s; 4 small squares is 0.16 s.
Hypokalaemia flattens T waves and may produce U waves; it does not peak them.
Correct: peaked T waves with weakness in kidney injury point to hyperkalaemia and Na⁺ channel inactivation.
Hypercalcaemia mainly shortens the QT interval; it does not peak T waves.
The rate is about 71/min (1,500 ÷ 21), not a tachycardia.

interpret.title: Observations after a head injury
rows: Left 5 mm sluggish, right 3 mm reactive
interpret.q: A 30-year-old cyclist hit his head two hours ago. Over the last hour he has become drowsy. Observations (typical adult ranges given for reference) are shown. What do these observations most suggest?
options: Rising intracranial pressure with a Cushing response
interpret.why: Rising blood pressure with a widening pulse pressure (190/80, so 110 mmHg), a slow pulse, irregular breathing and falling GCS is the Cushing response, a late sign of raised intracranial pressure from an expanding mass such as an extradural haematoma. It needs immediate senior help and urgent CT of the head.
optWhy: Vasovagal syncope causes transient bradycardia with low blood pressure and rapid recovery.
Sepsis typically causes fever, tachycardia and hypotension.
Falling GCS after a head injury is never normal recovery and needs urgent assessment.
Hypovolaemic shock causes a fast pulse and low blood pressure, the opposite of this picture.
Correct: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing and falling consciousness indicate raised ICP.

interpret.title: Numb feet and unsteady in the dark
interpret.q: A 68-year-old man who had a partial gastrectomy years ago has tingling feet and is unsteady, especially in the dark. Romberg's test is positive and vibration sense is absent at the ankles. Bloods are shown (typical adult UK ranges, which vary by lab). Which explanation fits best?
options: Iron deficiency causing a peripheral neuropathy
Vitamin B12 deficiency affecting the dorsal columns (and peripheral nerves)
interpret.why: Macrocytic anaemia (Hb 102 g/L, MCV 112 fL) with a low B12 after gastrectomy (loss of intrinsic factor) points to B12 deficiency. B12 deficiency can damage the dorsal columns (subacute combined degeneration), causing loss of vibration and proprioception and a sensory ataxia that worsens with the eyes closed, as Romberg's test shows.
optWhy: Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia, not an MCV of 112 fL.
Correct: macrocytosis with low B12 after gastrectomy and dorsal column signs.
Folate is normal here; folate deficiency (not excess) also causes macrocytosis.
Cerebellar ataxia is not worsened by closing the eyes (Romberg's test assesses proprioceptive, not cerebellar, ataxia), and B12 is low here.
TSH is normal, so hypothyroidism is unlikely.

interpret.title: Floppy weakness after diarrhoea
interpret.q: A 58-year-old has had severe diarrhoea for five days and now has generalised weakness with reduced tone and depressed reflexes but normal sensation. Bloods are shown (typical adult UK ranges, which vary by lab). Which explanation fits best?
options: An upper motor neuron lesion in the spinal cord
Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle membrane hyperpolarisation
interpret.why: Potassium is 2.1 mmol/L after heavy gastrointestinal loss. Low extracellular K⁺ makes E_K and the resting potential more negative, so muscle cells need a larger depolarisation to reach threshold and become weak and hypotonic, with reduced reflexes. Sensation is spared, and the deficit corrects as potassium is replaced. The ECG should be checked because hypokalaemia also affects cardiac repolarisation.
optWhy: A cord lesion would cause UMN signs (or spinal shock with a sensory level), not generalised weakness with normal sensation.
Adjusted calcium is normal here.
Guillain–Barré syndrome can follow a gut infection, but it usually brings sensory symptoms, and here a profound electrolyte cause is already shown.
Correct: K⁺ 2.1 mmol/L hyperpolarises muscle membranes and causes flaccid weakness.
Potassium is low, not high.

interpret.title: Lying and standing observations
rows: NICE: fall ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic is postural hypotension
interpret.q: A 78-year-old with Parkinson's disease has had two falls on getting out of bed. Lying and standing observations are shown. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Postural hypotension by systolic criteria, with a blunted heart-rate response
Postural hypotension by diastolic criteria only
The readings are uninterpretable without a 12-lead ECG
No postural hypotension, because standing systolic stays above 100 mmHg
interpret.why: Systolic falls from 136 to 108 mmHg (28 mmHg, at least 20 mmHg) and diastolic from 78 to 70 mmHg (8 mmHg), so the systolic criterion of NICE NG136 is met. Heart rate rises by only 4/min, suggesting autonomic failure, which is common in Parkinson's disease; dopaminergic and antihypertensive medicines should also be reviewed.
optWhy: Correct: 28 mmHg systolic fall with only a 4/min rise in heart rate.
The diastolic fall is 8 mmHg, below the 10 mmHg threshold; it is the systolic criterion that is met.
Postural tachycardia syndrome involves a large rise in heart rate without hypotension; here heart rate barely changes.
Postural blood pressure is interpreted from the readings themselves; an ECG adds information but is not needed for this.
The definition depends on the size of the fall, not the absolute standing value.

interpret.title: Memory clinic blood screen
interpret.q: A 74-year-old is referred with six months of slowed thinking, poor memory, low mood, weight gain and feeling cold. Before a dementia diagnosis, routine bloods are checked (typical adult UK ranges, which vary by lab). What do the results show?
options: Normal results: proceed to a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease
Primary hypothyroidism, a potentially reversible contributor to cognitive impairment
interpret.why: TSH is markedly raised (38 mU/L) with a low free T4 (6 pmol/L): primary hypothyroidism, which fits the slowing, low mood, weight gain and cold intolerance. Treatable causes such as thyroid disease, B12 or folate deficiency and metabolic disturbances are looked for with routine bloods before attributing cognitive decline to dementia; cognition is reassessed once the cause is treated.
optWhy: Adjusted calcium is within range.
The thyroid results are clearly abnormal, so this cannot be called a normal screen.
Correct: high TSH with low free T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism.
Hyperthyroidism gives a suppressed TSH with high free T4.
B12 is within range.

interpret.title: ECG after an antidepressant overdose
interpret.q: A 35-year-old took an unknown number of amitriptyline tablets. Lead II at 25 mm/s shows a regular rhythm with a P wave before each QRS. The R–R interval is 12 small squares and the QRS is 3.5 small squares wide. What is the best interpretation?
options: Atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate
Sinus rhythm at 75/min with normal QRS
Sinus tachycardia about 125/min with a broad QRS (about 0.14 s), consistent with sodium-channel blockade
interpret.why: R–R = 12 × 0.04 = 0.48 s, so the rate is 60 ÷ 0.48 = 125/min; P waves precede each QRS, so this is sinus tachycardia. QRS = 3.5 × 0.04 = 0.14 s, which is broad (normal under 0.12 s). In tricyclic overdose, tachycardia reflects antimuscarinic effects and the broad QRS reflects fast Na⁺ channel blockade, which predicts arrhythmias and seizures and needs urgent senior management.
optWhy: VT has no P waves before each complex, and the rate here is 125/min (250 would need an R–R of 6 small squares).
AF is irregularly irregular without P waves.
Complete heart block has a slow ventricular rate with P waves dissociated from QRS complexes.
75/min would need an R–R of 20 small squares, and a 0.14 s QRS is not normal.
Correct: rate 125/min, P before each QRS, QRS 0.14 s.

interpret.title: Lumbar puncture in a febrile, confused adult
rows: more than about half of plasma glucose
interpret.q: A 21-year-old student has fever, headache, neck stiffness and new confusion. There are no signs of raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture results are shown (typical adult values for reference, which vary by lab). Paired plasma glucose is 6.5 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
interpret.why: A very high white cell count that is mainly neutrophils, high protein and a CSF:plasma glucose ratio of 1.3 ÷ 6.5 = 0.2 (well below 0.5) is the typical bacterial pattern. NICE QS19 supports lumbar puncture without prior imaging when there is no contraindication, and treatment must not wait for results.
optWhy: Viral meningitis usually shows lymphocytes and a normal glucose ratio.
Correct: neutrophils, very high protein and a glucose ratio of 0.2.
TB meningitis often shows a mixed or lymphocytic picture with a more subacute history.
SAH gives red cells and xanthochromia, not a neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.
GBS gives high protein with a normal cell count and no fever or meningism.

interpret.title: Bedside spirometry in Guillain–Barré syndrome
rows: trend matters more than one value
interpret.q: A 44-year-old (weight 80 kg) admitted with Guillain–Barré syndrome has serial forced vital capacity measurements. Today he is weaker and his voice is quieter. What do these results show?
options: Stable respiratory function; no action needed
Progressive fall in FVC from about 54 to about 19 mL/kg, indicating neuromuscular respiratory failure needing urgent critical care review
interpret.why: FVC has fallen from 4.3 L (4.3 ÷ 80 ≈ 54 mL/kg) to 1.5 L (1.5 ÷ 80 ≈ 19 mL/kg). Serial FVC tracks respiratory muscle strength in neuromuscular disease; a fall towards about 20 mL/kg or below is a common trigger to consider ventilatory support (local protocols vary). Oxygen saturation stays normal until late, so it is falsely reassuring. He needs urgent critical care review.
optWhy: SpO₂ is preserved until late in neuromuscular respiratory failure.
A normal ratio with a small FVC indicates a restrictive (weakness) pattern, not improvement.
The FVC has fallen by about two-thirds; this is not stable.
Correct: falling FVC per kg indicates respiratory muscle failure.
FEV₁/FVC = 1.3 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 0.87, which is not obstructive; the problem is weakness.
